.github/scripts/check_skips.py -- Patch Q01: fail a CI job on an unexpected skip.

Why this exists.  pytest reports a skipped test as neither a pass nor a
failure, so a suite can go green while a whole group of tests quietly stops
running: the m2c job used to skip 3 schema-validation tests because
``jsonschema`` was not installed, and would have skipped about 22 grep tests
on any runner without ripgrep, and nobody would have been told.  This script
reads the JUnit XML report pytest writes (``--junitxml``), prints every skip
reason with a count, and exits non-zero unless every reason is on the allow
list in ``skip-allowlist.txt`` (same directory).

Usage (from a job, after pytest has written its report; the job must still
run this step when pytest failed or skipped, so use ``if: ${{ !cancelled() }}``):

    python .github/scripts/check_skips.py --scope m2c report.xml [report2.xml ...]

Options:
    --scope NAME       which allow-list entries apply: "m2c", "backend", or any
                       name.  Entries whose scope is "*" always apply.
    --allowlist FILE   default: skip-allowlist.txt next to this script.

Allow-list format (one entry per line, ``#`` starts a comment):

    scope | text that must appear in the skip reason [| when=ENV_VAR]

``when=ENV_VAR`` makes the entry active only while that environment variable is
exactly "1".  The m2c job uses it for the sandbox entry: the job probes whether
bubblewrap can create a user namespace on the runner and sets the variabl

.github/scripts/test_check_skips.py -- Patch Q01: tests for the skip gate.

check_skips.py is the CI step that turns "a test was skipped" from something a
person has to notice in a log into something that fails the job unless the
reason is on the allow list kept next to it (skip-allowlist.txt).  A gate that
can never fail is worse than no gate, so these tests pin the behaviour that
matters: an unlisted reason FAILS, and so does every input that would let a
problem pass quietly (a missing or unreadable report, a run in which no test
ran at all, an allow-list line the script cannot understand).

Standard library only, so it runs under the plain interpreter of any CI job:

    python -m pytest .github/scripts -q          (from the repository root)

Nothing here builds a secret-shaped string; every value is plain prose.

agents/code_editor.py — W5.2 (Build Workbench plan, step 204): the LLM
half of Chat's Edit mode. Given the person's instruction and the files /
line ranges they attached as chips (W4.1), it asks a model for D3-shaped
edits

    {"summary": str, "edits": [{"path", "op": "replace"|"create"|"delete",
                                "search", "replace", "content"}, ...]}

and hands them to eo/code_edit_apply.py's apply_edits(), which turns
them into per-file original/proposed text deterministically. The model
never writes a file the app trusts verbatim.

This module is eo/code_proposals.py's real `generate_edit` (the seam
that module's docstring describes — `create_proposal()` picks this up by
default, replacing `_stub_generate_edit`). Contract, unchanged from the
stub:

    generate_edit(ws_id, instruction, refs, current_files)
        -> {"summary": str, "files": [{"path", "op", "content"}, ...],
            "model_meta": dict}

`session_id` is an extra keyword-only argument create_proposal() binds
with functools.partial, so the call is attributed in Token Usage without
changing the contract every other replacement (tests, stubs) implements.
Anything that goes wrong raises CodeEditError; create_proposal() catches
that and stores a status='failed' proposal whose summary carries the
message, so the message is written for a person to read.

Master Blueprint).

Rewritten from the old OpenRouter/sequential version to match the blueprint
exactly:
- Provider: Cerebras only (no OpenRouter anywhere in this system).
- Concurrency: up to 5 modules written genuinely in parallel via
  ThreadPoolExecutor, one worker per Cerebras key (CEREBRAS_API_KEY_1..5).
- Model rotation: each worker cycles through 3 models in order if one
  fails -- gpt-oss-120b -> qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507 -> llama-4-scout-17b
  -- staying on its own assigned key throughout (workers don't share keys).

If there are more than 5 modules in a cycle, keys are reused round-robin
(modules 6, 7... share a key with modules 1, 2...) rather than failing --
an edge case the blueprint doesn't explicitly cover, but sharing beats
crashing.

generate_text() instead of a hand-rolled Cerebras client + retry loop, so
each worker's calls get usage-logged and fire usage_update events, same

agents/memory_search.py — Cross-Cycle Memory Search (Part 4, agent #0 of
the v5 Master Blueprint).

HuggingFace Inference (sentence-embedding) -> Upstash Vector (DB4).
No fallback listed in the blueprint for this one -- if HF Inference is
down, retrieval just degrades to "no prior context," which is safe (worse
planning, not a broken cycle), so this agent never raises to stop the loop.

Two jobs, both exposed as plain functions so other agents/loop.py can call
either independently:

  store_cycle_memory(cycle_num)  -- call AFTER report_writer.py, embeds this
      cycle's goal + summary + all_tests_passed, upserts into Vector under
      id "cyclemem:{app_slug}:{cycle_num}".

  retrieve_context(query_text, top_k=3) -- call BEFORE idea_planner.py,
      embeds the query (usually the original idea + current feature_status),
      queries Vector for the most similar past cycles FOR THIS APP ONLY
      (filtered by app_slug in metadata), returns a short text block ready
      to drop into idea_planner's prompt.

This agent is read-only with respect to Redis (DB1-3) -- it only ever reads
KEYS it needs and writes to KEYS["retrieved_context"] plus Vector itself.

agents/security_aggregator.py — Security Scan Aggregator (new; not one of
the original 19, same category as agents/review_aggregator.py: "agent #8,
deterministic Python, no LLM").

Closes a gap found via testing, not on the original blueprint list:
Scanner Pool (security_scanner.py) assigns ONE module per worker
(round-robin across 5 Cloudflare slots) -- unlike Reviewer Pool, where 3
workers redundantly look at ALL code and need de-duplication ACROSS
workers. Scanner Pool has no cross-worker duplication problem. What it
does have: a single Cloudflare call, for a single module, sometimes
listing the same underlying vulnerability twice in its own `findings`
list, phrased two different ways (e.g. "hardcoded secret in config" and
"API key exposed in source" for the same line of code). Nothing in
security_scanner.py de-duplicates a module's own findings list -- this
agent is that step.

HONEST LIMITATION, stated up front rather than glossed over: this is a
deterministic, no-LLM merge, so it can only catch duplicates that share
enough vocabulary to be detected by word-overlap -- see utils/similarity.py.
Two findings describing the same bug in completely disjoint wording (no
shared significant words at all) will NOT be caught. This trades recall
for the same "cheap and auditable" property review_aggregator.py
presumably already trades for on the Reviewer Pool side -- an LLM-based
semantic merge would catch more, at the cost of a 6th API call per module
and a new source of hallucinat

agents/source_planner_lean.py — Data Layer architecture §5b: Source
Planner (lean), Mode B's one judgment call.

Mode C (eo/source_index.py:get_packet(), §5a) is pure topic skeleton --
name/summary/parent/content_hint/covers, no LLM, no raw excerpt content.
That's enough for a purely structural consumer (§6a: Mind Mapper,
Concept Linker just draw the tree). It is NOT enough for a consumer
that needs to say something substantive ABOUT a topic's actual content
(§6b/§6c: Fact Detector, Note Table Builder, Study Generator, Workflow
Suggester) -- a one-line summary can't support pulling out a precise
fact or a workflow's real steps. Mode B is the middle ground: one small,
cheap LLM call looks at the skeleton ALONE (never the real source text)
and judges which topics are thin enough on their own that a consumer
would need the underlying excerpts pulled in too, and which are
detailed enough to answer from the skeleton as-is. Judgment only --
this module never generates the consumer's actual output, that's still
each retrofitted agent's own job in §6.

WHY "lean" here does NOT mean Part 2.4's tier-1 lean pipeline: that
pipeline (agents/prompt_writer_lean.py, code_writer_lean.py,
reviewer_fixer_lean.py) is a separate, fixed, memory-bus-KEYS-wired
sequence for tier-1's small-app coding path, with its own hardcoded
CHAIN that deliberately bypasses eo/registry.py's AGENT_CAPABILITIES
tagging. This role has nothing to do with that pipeline or that
product surface -- it's Notebooks' own do

agents/structure_architect.py — decides HOW the codebase should be organized
on disk. Does not touch the filesystem itself; it only outputs a plan of
operations that file_manager.py then executes mechanically.

Runs after Fixer+Tester, before file_manager.py.

Why this is its own agent and not just smarter code:
- Deciding whether a new module is a new file, belongs inside an existing
  file, needs its own subfolder, or makes an old file obsolete requires
  understanding the code's purpose -- a judgment call, not a string operation.
- Keeping it separate from file_manager.py means the LLM only ever proposes
  a plan (JSON); your own code is the only thing that ever writes, deletes,
  or moves files. If the model hallucinates a bad path, you can validate/
  reject the plan before anything touches disk.

Bug fix — two-mode planning: this used to hard-require `fixed_code` and
raise if it was empty, which made this agent (and file_manager.py
downstream) structurally unable to run for any task that doesn't produce
source code at all -- e.g. "build me a yearbook app with a folder per
year to keep memories in," which is a genuine, valid file/folder-
organizing request, not a coding one. The Inspector/Panel can (correctly)
decide a task needs "file_manager" without needing any code-writing role
at all; this agent shouldn't then be the thing that makes that
impossible.

Now genuinely two modes:

api/middleware.py — keeps unhandled server errors readable by the browser.

THE PROBLEM THIS EXISTS TO SOLVE
--------------------------------
Starlette builds the middleware stack as

    ServerErrorMiddleware -> [user middleware, e.g. CORSMiddleware] -> ExceptionMiddleware -> routes

`HTTPException`, `RequestValidationError` and every exception that has
its own `@app.exception_handler` (DatabaseUnavailable, AgentPoolSaturated,
AgentTaskTimeout in api/server.py) are answered by ExceptionMiddleware,
which sits INSIDE CORSMiddleware, so those responses get their
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header. An exception nobody handles (a
psycopg error, a plain bug) instead escapes all the way up to
ServerErrorMiddleware, the OUTERMOST layer, which writes its bare
"Internal Server Error" 500 from outside CORSMiddleware: no CORS
headers. The browser then refuses to expose that response to the page
and `fetch()` rejects with an opaque "TypeError: Failed to fetch" — so
every backend bug (e.g. the Build tab's move/rename hitting a database
permission error) looked like a connectivity problem, and the real
status code and message were invisible to the frontend.

(`@app.exception_handler(Exception)` does NOT help: Starlette routes
that one specifically to ServerErrorMiddleware too, so it has the same
problem.)

THE FIX
-------
UnhandledErrorMiddleware sits just INSIDE CORSMiddleware. It catches
whatever the routes/ExceptionMiddleware didn't handle and answers with a
JSON 500 in the same `{"de

api/routes/code_runs.py -- Patch S10: "grant more" for an M2C run that stopped at its credit ceiling.

    POST /v1/code/runs/{run_id}/grant        Authorization: Bearer <device JWT>        (no body)
         -> 200 {state: "running", run_credit_ceiling, run_credits_spent, granted_credits}

WHO CALLS IT. The device, with the same short-lived device JWT it gets from POST /v1/code/devices/token (S03). The
terminal shows the user "this run reached its credit limit; grant more?", and on a yes it calls this route. The web
app's session tokens are not accepted here: only a token whose type is `device` and whose device is live (the
verification, eo.devices.verify_device_token, checks both and that the device was not revoked).

WHAT A GRANT IS. A run in `paused_budget` goes back to `running` with a raised per-run ceiling (one chunk more than it
had already spent: codeagent/metering.py's RunCeilingPolicy decides how big a chunk is) and its turn is restarted. It
does NOT raise the account's pool: the pool is the account's plan, shared with the web app, and is only ever read here.
A grant while the pool is empty is refused (`quota_exhausted`, with the reset time) and changes nothing.

THE ORDER (every step before the claim only reads; every step after it is undone if it fails)

    2  the run is this account's AND this device's     404 run_not_found, the same body as a run that does not exi

api/routes/devices.py -- S03: the HTTP surface for M2C device pairing.

Two audiences, one router (mounted with a single include_router line in
api/server.py):

  The terminal (`m2c login`, no account session yet) -- /v1/code/devices/*
    POST /v1/code/devices/pair/start   {device_name, os, client_version}
         -> {device_code, user_code, verification_url, interval, expires_in}
    POST /v1/code/devices/pair/poll    {device_code}
         -> {status: pending | approved | denied | expired}; `approved` also
            carries {device_credential, device_id}, exactly once.
            An unknown or already-collected device_code is a 400.
    POST /v1/code/devices/token        {device_credential}
         -> {jwt, expires_in}   (a ~15 minute device JWT; 401 if the
            credential is unknown or the device was revoked)

  The signed-in web app (require_auth, the usual Supabase bearer) -- /api/devices*
    POST /api/devices/approve          {user_code} -> binds the terminal to the caller
    POST /api/devices/deny             {user_code} -> refuses it ("not my terminal")
    GET  /api/devices[?include_revoked=true]
                                       -> {devices: [...]}, the caller's own, active only by default
    POST /api/devices/{id}/revoke      -> {id, revoked_at}; 404 for anyone else's device

All the decisions live in eo/devices.py (read its docstring first); this
file only turns its outcomes into status codes. Status mapping:

    429  too many attempts: pair/

Run locally:
    pip install fastapi uvicorn
    uvicorn api.server:app --reload --port 8000

CORS is open to the Next.js dev server origin (localhost:3000) only —

api/stream_tickets.py

Short-lived, single-use tickets for the two browser transports that can't
send an Authorization header: the /ws/{session_id} WebSocket and the
/api/task/{session_id}/stream EventSource (SSE).

Why this exists
---------------
Neither `new WebSocket(url)` nor `new EventSource(url)` lets the page set
request headers, so both used to carry the user's full Supabase access
token as `?token=<jwt>`. A query string is the one part of a request that
reliably ends up in places a header doesn't: uvicorn/proxy/CDN access
logs, Sentry breadcrumbs, browser history. A leaked access token is a
bearer credential for the *whole* API for as long as it lives (about an
hour), not just for the stream it was minted for.

How it works
------------
1. The page calls `POST /api/stream-ticket` (ordinary Authorization
   header, see api/routes/stream_ticket.py) saying which transport and
   which session_id it wants to open.
2. We mint a random ticket, store {user_id, kind, session_id} under the
   ticket's SHA-256 for TICKET_TTL_SECONDS, and hand the raw ticket back.
3. The page opens the socket/stream with `?ticket=<ticket>`.
4. The stream route redeems it with an atomic GETDEL: it is valid for one
   redemption only, even if two requests race, and expires on its own if
   nobody redeems it.

What a leaked ticket is worth: nothing after first use or ~30 seconds,
and it only ever opens the one transport/session it was minted for.

Design choices worth knowing
---------------------

Hugging Face embedding cold-start check.

Mirrors utils/embedding.py's embed_text() EXACTLY (same URL, same payload,
same wait_for_model flag, same timeout) so this reproduces what your app
actually experiences -- not a simplified version of it.

Run from your backend folder (same venv as the app):
    python check_hf_embedding.py

Makes the SAME call twice, back-to-back:
  - Call #1: if the model is currently unloaded on HF's shared inference
    infra, this is the one that pays the cold-start cost. wait_for_model=True
    means HF holds the connection open and waits rather than erroring, so a
    slow-but-successful response here (many seconds, possibly close to a
    minute) is the cold-start tax landing.
  - Call #2: run immediately after #1. If the model is now warm, this
    should come back in well under a second. A big gap between call #1 and
    call #2 is the confirmation.

codeagent -- the server side of M2C (the `m2c` terminal client's brain).

Named `codeagent`, not `m2c`, so it can never clash with the top-level `m2c/`
client package when both sit in one dev environment (build plan O5).

Patch S04 creates this package with the device socket (ws.py, connections.py).
Later patches add modules beside them (the model adapter, the run manager, the
tool broker); this file stays empty of imports on purpose, so importing a
sibling never drags in the socket or its dependencies.

codeagent/adapters/ -- model adapters for the M2C server (patch S05).

One module per provider family, all speaking the provider-neutral interface
defined in codeagent/model_adapter.py:

    openai_compat.py   OpenAI-compatible chat completions with native tool use
                       (Groq, Mistral, Gemini's OpenAI layer, the Hugging Face
                       router, OpenRouter, or any other base URL). First adapter,
                       build plan decision D3. An Anthropic adapter is second and
                       a Gemini-native one third; they are separate patches.
    toolcalls.py       Tolerant tool-call parsing, ported from MiniLocker
                       (decision D12). Pure functions, no network.

Nothing is imported here on purpose. `import codeagent.adapters.toolcalls`
must stay cheap and must not drag in the OpenAI SDK, `utils.llm_client` (and
through it Redis, the database layer and every provider SDK) or any other
heavy module; import the module you need explicitly.

NAMESPACE NOTE. This patch deliberately does not create backend/codeagent/
__init__.py: patch S04 creates it in parallel. Until both are applied
`codeagent` is a plain namespace package, which is enough for
`from codeagent.adapters import toolcalls` and for the tests under
backend/tests/unit/test_codeagent_*.py to import it. Once S04's file exists
it becomes a regular package and nothing here changes.

codeagent/adapters/openai_compat.py -- OpenAI-compatible chat completions with native tool use (patch S05,
decision D3). Streams `text_delta`, `tool_call` and `usage` events (codeagent/model_adapter.py).

WHICH PROVIDERS. Anything that speaks OpenAI's /chat/completions with `tools` and `stream=True`: Groq, Mistral,
Gemini's OpenAI layer, the Hugging Face router, OpenRouter, or any other base URL. These are exactly the providers
utils/llm_client.py already has client factories for, and this adapter reuses those (see KEY SELECTION).

HOW A CALL RUNS
  * The request goes out with `stream=True` and `stream_options={"include_usage": True}`; if an SDK version rejects
    the second kwarg (TypeError) it is retried without, and usage then comes from wherever the provider puts it or
    is reported as unreported (never an error: metering fails open).
  * The provider SDKs here are synchronous. A daemon worker thread iterates the SDK stream and hands chunks to the
    event loop through an asyncio.Queue (the same bridge utils/llm_client.py's _walk_chain_once_stream uses, but one
    dedicated thread per stream instead of the shared executor, so a long stream can never starve other work and
    cannot keep the interpreter alive at shutdown). All parsing happens on the loop side, single-threaded.
  * Closing the async generator, or cancelling the task that iterates it, sets a stop flag and closes the HTTP
    stream; the worker exits. That is how a run's `cancel` reaches the provider.

files.module_doc:
Tolerant tool-call handling, for models that do not honour the OpenAI tool-calling contract to the letter.

Three things go wrong in practice, and this module fixes each one:

  * the structured call is *almost* right: arguments wrapped in a code fence, a trailing comma, single
    quotes, a `functions.` prefix on the name, or an object where a JSON string belongs;
  * the provider rejects a malformed call with HTTP 400 `tool_use_failed` but hands back what the model
    wrote (`failed_generation`), and that text is usually a perfectly clear call in another syntax;
  * the model writes the call as *text* in its own native syntax (Hermes `<tool_call>`, Llama `<function=..>`,
    Kimi `<|tool_call_begin|>`, gpt-oss "harmony", ReAct, or bare JSON) instead of using the structured field.

Everything here is pure (no network, no Docker), so it is cheap to test exhaustively.

Rules that keep this safe. Model output is untrusted, and parsing free text for "a tool call" is exactly the
place where a prompt injection could be promoted into an action, so the parser is conservative:

  1. Only text that *consists of* tool-call markup counts. Prose that merely quotes some JSON (a summary of a
     hostile page, say) is not a call. Protocol-token formats tolerate a short preamble; free-form JSON and
     ReAct do not. The one relaxation is `failed_generation`, where the provider has already decided the text
     was an attempted call.
  2. Reasoning blocks (`<think>...</think>`) are removed

codeagent/broker.py -- S09: the server tool broker.

The agent loop (S07) decides the model wants a tool run. The tool runs on the user's DEVICE,
under the device's own policy. The broker is the one place on the server that carries that
exchange: it proposes the call to the connected device, waits for the answer, and turns
whatever happens (a result, a denial, silence, a lost connection, a cancel) into exactly one
outcome for the loop and exactly one `tool_finished` event for the device's stream.

    loop (S07)  --propose(...)-->  broker  --tool_proposed-->  emit  -->  device
                <--ToolOutcome---          <--tool_result / approval / tool_stream--  (router, S14)

THE CALL LIFECYCLE (protocol/README.md sections 2, 3 and 5)
-----------------------------------------------------------
    1. propose(): the broker registers the call and emits `tool_proposed` {call_id, tool,
       input, risk}: a STREAM message, so it carries a seq, which the emitter assigns.
    2. The device's policy decides. It answers with `approval` {call_id, decision, scope} when
       a decision was made, and with `tool_result` {call_id, ok, output, truncated, trust, ...}
       if it ran the tool. A DENIED call gets an approval with decision `deny` and NO
       tool_result: the broker finishes it at once instead of waiting for a timeout.
    3. The call ends exactly once, with one `run_event tool_finished` {call_id, tool, status,
       duration_ms}. status is one of:

           ok

codeagent/buffer.py -- S06 (part b): the ephemeral, encrypted run buffer.

While a run is active the server must keep two things so the loop can call the model
and so a device that drops can come back (build plan section O1, "Server, ephemeral
content"):

  * the CONVERSATION: the run's state (profile, mode, instructions, ...) and every
    history item, so the next model call can be built and prompt-cache prefixes stay
    stable;
  * the REPLAY EVENTS: every stream message (run_event, tool_proposed, budget_warning)
    the server sent to the device, stored VERBATIM, so run.resume{last_seq} can
    re-deliver everything after last_seq with the same id and seq (protocol/README.md
    section 5). They carry reply text and tool output, so they are content too.

Both live ONLY here: in Redis, through the existing Upstash client (memory.bus.redis),
encrypted with AES-GCM, expiring, and deleted when the run ends. Never Postgres, never a
log line. runs.py (S06 part a) is the content-free record of the same run; this module is
the content half and never touches that table.

WHERE THIS SITS
---------------
    ws.py (S04)      hands run-scoped messages to the installed MessageHandler
    S14              the router that is that handler
    runs.py (S06a)   the run row and its state machine
    buffer.py (here) the encrypted conversation + replay buffer
    S06c             glues the two (delete on a terminal state, run_guard cancel keys,
                     expire_stale, run.resume

codeagent/connections.py -- S04: who is connected to the device socket right now,
and how to talk to them.

Three small pieces, each behind an interface the later patches build on:

  DeviceConnection   one authenticated socket: who it is, a serialized send path
                     that builds protocol/v1 envelopes, and an idempotent close.
                     S06 (run manager) and S09 (tool broker) hold one of these and
                     call send_message()/send_error(); they never touch the
                     WebSocket itself.
  ConnectionRegistry the connected devices per user. InMemoryRegistry is the only
                     implementation for now. It holds LIVE SOCKETS OF THIS PROCESS,
                     which can never leave process memory, so its methods are
                     plain synchronous calls. S11 (process split) keeps this
                     registry as the gateway's local table and adds cross-process
                     presence ("is this device online anywhere") on top, in Redis.
                     That is why callers go through get_registry() and never
                     import InMemoryRegistry directly.
  HandshakeLimiter   a per-address budget for FAILED handshakes. In memory, behind
                     get_handshake_limiter(); S11 can swap in a Redis-backed one.

None of this module logs: it handles message content on its way to a socket.

prompts.DefaultContextAssembler. It keeps the same interface, `assemble(state, items, tools, mode) ->

codeagent/emitter.py -- S14 (part b): numbered, stored, delivered server events.

Everything the server streams to a device about a run (reply text, tool proposals, state
changes, budget warnings) is a numbered message: protocol/README.md section 5 says the
server numbers its run stream 1, 2, 3 ... with no gaps, keeps every message so a device
that dropped can ask for the ones it missed, and re-delivers them verbatim. This module is
the one place that does the numbering, the keeping and the sending, so the loop (S07), the
tool broker (S09) and the handlers (S14c-e) never have to agree on how.

    ws.py (S04)        the socket: authenticated, validated; a connection to send on
    router.py          S14a: dispatch by message type
    emitter.py (here)  number it, store it (encrypted), send it if the device is there
    run_handlers.py    S14c-e: calls the emitter around every state change
    buffer.py (S06b)   the encrypted replay stream and the stream counter (next_seq)

ONE EMIT = THREE STEPS, IN THIS ORDER, UNDER ONE LOCK
-----------------------------------------------------
    1. number   seq = buffer.next_seq(run_id)           the counter lives in Redis
    2. store    buffer.append_replay(run_id, envelope)  encrypted, verbatim
    3. send     connection.send_json(envelope)          only if the device is connected

Steps 1 and 2 run in ONE worker-thread call, so a caller that is cancelled between them
cannot burn a seq number (next_seq cannot be given back). Storing co

WHAT THIS IS. Two small things the agent loop (loop.py) needs and that must not live in it:

  1. The SYSTEM PROMPT (product guide 6.4). Short, capability-focused, written as judgement and not as a
     rule list: what the agent is, that it works through tools, that the person may refuse a call and a
     refused action is not retried unasked, and that file contents and tool results are DATA, never
     instructions. Tool usage lives in the tool descriptions (protocol/v1/tools), not here, and there are no
     examples (they narrow how a model explores). It says nothing about internal configuration: no
     environment variable, no server path, no provider, no limit. Tests pin its length and that.

     model request and does not care how it is built. DefaultContextAssembler is the simple v0 version:
     system prompt, then the person's instructions, matched rules and memory index (all CONTENT the client
     sent in run.start), then the conversation (history, replies, tool calls, tool results), with the tool
     schemas passed alongside. S08 (context assembler v0 proper: budgets, caching, compaction) replaces it
     by passing its own object to the loop; nothing in loop.py changes.

codeagent/router.py -- S14 (part a): the message router.

S04's socket (ws.py) authenticates and validates, then hands every message other than
`ping` to ONE installed MessageHandler (ws.set_message_handler). This module is that
handler. It does one thing: look at the message's type `t` and give the message to the
function registered for it. What those functions do (start a run, queue a turn, cancel,
resume, pause on disconnect) is S14c-e's; how their events reach the device is S14b's.

    ws.py (S04)        authenticated, validated, rate-limited connection
    router.py (here)   dispatch by message type; contain a handler's mistakes
    emitter.py         S14b: numbered, stored, delivered server events
    run_handlers.py    S14c-e: the handlers that are registered here
    run_manager.py     S06: start, resume, pause, end, cancel

THE RULES
---------
* Dispatch is by `msg["t"]`, nothing else. The router never reads a payload: it cannot
  leak what it does not look at, and it cannot get a payload wrong.
* A message type with no registered handler is answered with the protocol error
  `internal`, with the message's id as ref_id and a fixed text (MSG_NO_HANDLER). Never
  silence: a device that sends something nobody handles must not wait for it.
  (The code is `internal` because the protocol has no "not implemented"; the message is
  valid, so `invalid_message` would blame the client for a server gap.)
* A handler that raises is CONTAINED. The exception's TYPE is logged, the

S05/S06/S07/S09. What it gives them is an authenticated, validated, rate-limited
connection and a seam to plug into (MessageHandler, below).

HANDSHAKE (protocol/v1/hello.json, welcome.json)
-------------------------------------------------
    device                                         server
    ------                                         ------
    connect ---------------------------------->    accept (so errors can be answered in v1 shape)
    hello{protocol_versions, device_credential,
          client_version, capabilities} ------->   within hello_timeout_s, and it must be a hello
                                                   validate the envelope and payload against protocol/v1
                                                   pick the highest version both sides speak
                                                   authenticate the credential (eo/devices.py, S03)
                                    <------------  welcome{protocol, min_protocol, token_ttl_s,
                                                           limits, server_version}
    ... run.start, user_message, ping, ...   <-->  validate

eo/code_edit_apply.py — W5.2 (Build Workbench plan, step 204): the
deterministic half of the code-edit pipeline. agents/code_editor.py
asks a model for edits in the plan's D3 shape

    {"summary": str, "edits": [{"path", "op": "replace"|"create"|"delete",
                                "search", "replace", "content"}, ...]}

and THIS module — pure functions, no LLM, no database, no I/O of any

The model never produces a whole file to be trusted verbatim; it points
at a `search` block and this module decides, deterministically,
whether and where that block lands.

    project's stylesheets — the change for those is in the element's own
    `className`, which is already in the model's view.

eo/concurrency_gate.py — Phase 4 of the reliability overhaul (see
reliability_overhaul_plan.md §PHASE 4, Patch B).

Patch A (utils/rate_ledger.py's reserve()/release_reservation()) closed
the race INSIDE a single gated LLM call: can_proceed() used to only read,
so two concurrent callers could both see "headroom free" before either
one's usage got booked. reserve() folds the check and the provisional
booking into one call, shrinking that race to one bus round trip.

This module is the layer above that: the fan-out sites themselves
(agents/hardware_speccer.py's _populate_prices(), eo/executor.py's
_run_concurrent_group()) don't currently ask the ledger anything before
deciding how many threads to start — they size a ThreadPoolExecutor to a
FIXED count (len(key_envs), len(group_roles), ...) and let every thread
race into its own call, each individually discovering via Patch A's
reserve() that there wasn't room after all, and each individually
sleeping/rerouting inside utils/llm_client.py's retry loop. That still
converges (Patch A prevents any of them from overshooting the ledger),
but it wastes a burst of started-then-blocked threads, adds pointless
per-thread sleep/retry latency, and gives the pool no way to adapt when
headroom frees up mid-run — the exact "7 parallel part_price_finder
workers all pile onto whichever accounts they were handed at t=0,
whether or not those accounts have room" scenario named in the incident
log this phase traces back to.

run_gated() is the fix:

eo/credits.py -- S02: cost-weighted credits for one model call.

    credits_for(provider, model, input, cached_input, output) -> float

turns one call's token counts into credits (Build Plan section O2, Decision
D5). The point of "cost-weighted" is the agent loop: a coding agent re-sends
a large, mostly cached prompt at every step and gets a short reply, so
counting raw tokens would drain the shared pool far faster than the call
really costs, and ignoring the cache discount would overcharge it. Each
class of token is priced separately, in USD per million tokens:

    input        prompt tokens that were NOT served from the provider's cache
    cached_input prompt tokens served from the cache (the "cached read" price)
    output       generated tokens

TOKEN CONVENTION (the one callers must follow)
----------------------------------------------
`input` is the TOTAL prompt tokens of the call, INCLUDING the cached ones;
`cached_input` is the part of that total that came from the cache. So

    cached   = min(cached_input, input)
    uncached = input - cached            (= max(input - cached_input, 0))

and uncached + cached always equals `input`. This is the OpenAI-compatible
shape (usage.prompt_tokens includes usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens)

eo/data_handler.py — Patch C2 (MiniMe-Patch-Series-C-Plan.md, Track 2):
the command-string front door onto eo/data_store.py.

One function, run_data_command(session_id, command), is the only thing
agents actually call. It looks like a command string because that's a
compact, model-fluent format for an LLM to emit — not because anything
resembling a real shell sits underneath it. Underneath, it's a small

input never raises past this function — it comes back as a short

run_data_command()'s own return type (str) implies, and the same
"denial comes back as data, not an exception" posture
eo/introspection.py's functions use for their own error case (see that
module's docstring) — just returned as a formatted string here instead
of a dict, since this function's whole job is producing text for a
model's context window.

section-addressable storage for per-task artifact data.

Same shape discipline as eo/secondary_data.py (one JSON document per
key, a lock around read-modify-write) but generalized to arbitrary
free-form text sections instead of that module's topic-tree schema.

what patch_section()'s optional `expected_version` is for — see its
own docstring.

eo/devices.py -- S03: M2C device pairing and device credentials.

`m2c login` links a terminal to a MiniMe account without ever typing a
password into it. This module is the whole server-side state machine
behind that, in the shape of the OAuth device-code flow (RFC 8628):

    terminal                                   web app (signed in)
    --------                                   -------------------
    start_pairing()  -> device_code (secret),
                        user_code  (BCDF-GHJK),
                        verification_url
    shows the user code
                                               person types the code
                                               approve_pairing(user, code)
    poll_pairing(device_code) ... pending ...
    poll_pairing(device_code) -> approved +
                        device_credential (ONCE) + device_id
    stores the credential in the OS keychain

    later, every ~15 minutes, and on every reconnect:
    issue_device_token(credential) -> short-lived JWT
    (sub = user id, device_id), which S04's socket handshake presents
    and checks with verify_device_token().

Tables are in migration 0013 (devices, device_pairings), which keeps what
must never change (a device's owner and credential hash, a pairing's codes
and expiry, a revocation) immutable with triggers rather than column grants.

codes, headers) lives there; everything that decides live

eo/dispatcher.py — deterministic routing engine.

Migration Part 12 §3.2: this REPLACES next_step() from Parts 2/8/9/11
entirely. This is the final version.

Why the rewrite: Part 2's next_step() matched a "next" destination
string against `agent_names` (resolved module names) to find where to
jump. That broke the moment `generic_worker` started running for many
different roles in the same plan (Part 10 §2's REAL_ACTION_ROLES split)
— with coding now unified into the same pipeline (Part 12 §0), that
includes early coding stages too (idea_planner/prompt_writer aren't
real-action roles, so they resolve to "generic_worker" same as
brainstormer/writer). A "NEXT: prompt_writer" tag had no way to
disambiguate which generic_worker SLOT in agent_names it meant, since
multiple slots are all literally the string "generic_worker".

The fix: index everything by role_names (the ordered list of ROLE names
for this run — NOT resolved module names), and only resolve to a module
name at the moment eo/executor.py actually calls the function. This
module now returns an INDEX into role_plan, not a destination string —
the caller (executor.py) resolves agent_names[next_idx] separately to
know which function to call.

Also renamed per the field this now reads: agents emit "next_destination"
(a role name), not the old "next" (a resolved module/destination name).

eo/graph_edges.py — knowledge-graph edges (Part 0, Section 0.2).

Nodes (Section 0.1) live in Upstash Vector under the `node:{workspace_id}:
{node_id}` id-prefix convention, because they're semantically searchable
content. Edges are NOT semantically searchable — they're structured
relationships — so they belong in a small JSON store instead, same shape
as eo/chat_workspace.py's _workspaces.json and eo/memory_batch.py's
_batches.json: a single file, a lock around read/modify/write, one array
of records.

`relation` is deliberately a free-form string, not a fixed enum — same
philosophy as eo/routing_memory.py's `outcome` field. "supports", "cites",
"contradicts", "promoted_from", etc. are all valid without pre-defining
every possible relationship type up front.

Two ways an edge gets created (matching the blueprint's own distinction):
  - Auto-created: an agent that consumes one node while producing another
    calls create_edge() itself, right after it writes the new node (same
    discipline agents/dependency_mapper.py already follows for code
    modules — recorded at the moment the relationship is known, not
    guessed after the fact).
  - Manually created: a UI affordance (drag node onto node, or a "link
    to..." picker) hits a `create_edge` endpoint that also just calls
    create_edge() below. No agent involvement needed for this path.

eo/integrations.py — Part 8.5: shared per-user OAuth credential storage.

One table, one module, for every third-party connector (Calendar, Gmail,
Slack, Jira/Asana/Linear, ...) — same reasoning as eo/audit_log.py being
one table for every mutating action rather than one table per domain.
Each connector agent (agents/calendar_agent.py being the first) calls
get_credentials()/refresh_if_needed() to get a live access token; it never
touches the user_integrations table directly.

Deliberately thin, same discipline as every other module in this
migration: plain functions, owner_id-scoped queries, no ORM. Callers
(api/server.py's OAuth routes) decide who's allowed to call these; this
module just stores and retrieves.

--- Token encryption -------------------------------------------------------
access_token/refresh_token are stored Fernet-encrypted, key from
INTEGRATIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY (a standalone key — deliberately NOT reusing
SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET or SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, so rotating one never
silently affects the other). Generate one with:
    python -c "from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())"
and set it in the server's env. If this key is ever rotated, every stored
token becomes unreadable and every user must reconnect — there is no
re-encryption migration here; that's out of scope for this pass and
should be flagged if it ever becomes a real operational need.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

pre-gate for the two routing decisions that currently cost extra LLM

WHY THESE TWO ARE DIFFERENT FROM TIER 2 (eo/sga.py's pre-gate)
Tier 2's error is one-sided-safe: a wrong "skip SGA" only loses a fast
shortcut, never quality. These two are NOT:
  - The panel is the safety net for the Inspector's known failure mode --
    a task worded to SOUND trivial that implies multi-module scope (see
    the Inspector's own SYSTEM_PROMPT: "the case most likely to be
    under-routed"). Skipping it wrongly means under-routing.
  - A wrong gatekeeper STOP ends a build one improvement pass early.

existing LLM path still decides, and the verdict is scored against what
the LLM path then actually decided (get_panel_gate_stats()/
get_gatekeeper_gate_stats()). Only after those numbers look good should
you flip a gate to "on". An untuned Laya is a weak judge of this kind of
question (it inverted a similar one in Tier 1 testing), so treat "on" as
something to earn with data, not a default.

HTTP), NOT the daemon's custom websocket protocol in
eo/local_workspace.py -- see docs/decisions/0001-cli-skills-mcp-scope.md

eo/memory_batch.py — named, mutual-membership groups of chats that share
memory with EACH OTHER (unlike chat_store.set_linked_chats, which is
one-directional per chat). A batch is the "group of 5 linked chats" the UI
shows as one unit.

Relationship to chat_store.linked_chat_ids: creating/editing a batch is
the ONLY thing that should write linked_chat_ids for its members going
forward — it keeps every member's linked_chat_ids in sync so membership
stays symmetric. Chats not in a batch can still use the old manual
per-chat linking UI if you want to keep that power-user path available.

--- Part 8.2 migration notes -----------------------------------------------
Migrated from data/chats/_batches.json to Postgres (batches +
batch_members tables, see part8_schema.sql), scoped by owner_id. Every
function now takes owner_id, slotted in right after any existing
identifier argument — same convention as chat_store.py / chat_workspace.py.

Behavior tightening vs. the old file version: member_chat_ids passed to
create_batch/add_member are now filtered down to chat IDs that actually
exist AND are owned by owner_id before being stored (batch_members has a
real foreign key to chats). The old version would silently store bogus
IDs in member_chat_ids itself and only the downstream linking ignored
them — this closes that gap rather than reproducing it, matching the
same filter chat_store.set_linked_chats already applies elsewhere.
--------------------------------------------------------------

eo/plans.py -- S01: which plan is an account on, how big is its credit
pool, and what period does that pool cover right now?

Two sources, in this order:

  1. The account's row in `user_plans` (migration 0012), if it has one.
     The row is authoritative for its own pool: `credit_pool` is stored
     per account so a support top-up or grant changes one account without
     changing the plan definition, and `plan_key` is only the label.
  2. config/plans.json's defaults, for an account with no row ("Free and
     unconfigured accounts follow plans.json defaults"): the default
     plan's pool over a calendar-month window (UTC).

There is no billing job in this codebase yet, so a stored period can end
without anything advancing it. Rather than letting an account's pool
silently stay "used up" forever (or reset to nothing), the effective
window is rolled forward by whole months from the stored period_start --
the billing-anniversary rule from Rulebook section 7.2 -- without writing
anything back. When billing eventually does write the new period, the
stored value and the rolled value agree.

A 'canceled' plan falls back to the default plan's pool: the account is
still usable, it is just no longer entitled to what it stopped paying
for. 'past_due' keeps its pool; whether to cut it off is a billing
decision, not something to infer here.

"why the denylist needs two forms").

The denylist has two halves, and they are deliberately NOT the same
mechanism:

  - The *documentation* half lives in eo/capability_entries.py, as
    entry_type="redaction" rows in the same registry:capability_entries
    store Patch B1 introduced for capability entries. It's
    human-editable and visible — the place to jot down a new redaction
    the moment someone thinks of it ("don't let an agent read
    config/prod_keys.json"), the same way you'd add a line to a
    checklist. Because it's just data, a model can write to it,
    misread it, or (if something upstream goes wrong) ignore it.

  - This module is the *enforcement* half. It is hard-coded Python —
    not data, not something write_capability_entry() can touch — so
    that "a path is unreadable" does not depend on any row existing,
    surviving, or being interpreted correctly in a data store the
    model itself has write access to. Patch B4's introspection.py
    calls is_readable() here before returning any file content,
    directory listing, or search hit; it does NOT consult
    capability_entries.py's redaction rows to decide readability,
    because the whole point of a hard-coded check is that it holds
    even if that data is empty, wrong, or maliciously permissive.

where a human (or an agent, on a human's behalf) writes dow

eo/run_guard.py -- per-run safety rails for the agent pipeline.

Why this exists (audit, 2026-09-25): a task that hit repeated errors kept
running in the background long after the HTTP request had already been
answered (or had timed out), burning rate limit on roles that could not
succeed, and the macro-loop then re-ran the whole graph. Three independent
rails fix that, all keyed by session_id and all cheap to check:

1. CANCEL FLAG  -- request_cancel(session_id, reason). Checked at every LLM
   chain step (utils/llm_client.py) and at every role boundary
   (eo/executor.py). When the HTTP layer gives up on a request (deadline,
   client stop button) it sets this flag so the orphaned worker thread
   actually stops instead of running for another half hour.

2. FAILURE BREAKER -- record_role_outcome(). N consecutive failed roles (or M
   failed roles in total) trips the breaker. The executor then pauses the run
   for manual approval instead of grinding through the rest of the graph.

3. TOKEN BUDGET -- like an agent hitting its tool-call limit and asking the
   user whether to keep going. Every LLM call's real token usage is added to
   the session's counter (utils/llm_client.py::_log_usage). When the counter
   crosses the soft budget the executor pauses at the next role boundary
   (reason "token_budget_exceeded"); POST /api/resume {"action": "approve"}
   grants another chunk and continues. A hard ceiling (soft x HARD_FACTOR)
   stops even a single runaway role mid-flight.

eo/spec_cache.py — plain TTL cache for component_spec_lookup.py results.

Same memory.bus read/write mechanism eo/price_cache.py already uses --
no new storage layer -- but a much longer TTL: unlike price_cache.py's
5-day window (prices genuinely move), a real part's physical
dimensions_mm/datasheet_url don't change once DigiKey or Mouser has
confirmed them. TTL here exists purely as a self-healing safety net
(a wrong parse getting fixed and needing to eventually re-populate,
a datasheet link going stale) rather than because the underlying data
is expected to drift -- so it's set to 180 days, not price_cache.py's
5.

Keeps DigiKey/Mouser quota usage low across repeated project
generations that reuse common parts (ESP32, common sensors, etc.) --
the same reasoning price_cache.py's own docstring gives for prices.

Only successful lookups are cached (get_real_spec() writes here only
after a real DigiKey/Mouser hit) -- a miss (part not found on either
vendor, or creds unset) is cheap enough, and ambiguous enough per-part
number, not to be worth caching as a standing negative result the way
price_cache.py caches an empty listings=[] search.

The langfuse v4 SDK (pinned in requirements.txt) is safe to call even when
no credentials are configured: get_client() internally falls back to a

non-trivial work to build a payload (e.g. serializing a large prompt/

check this flag first and skip the work entirely. Nothing needs it for
correctness, only to avoid wasted work when tracing is off.

chain, where no user id is in scope and none is passed down (see

     those calls would be metered as 'system'. A binding lasts exactly as
     long as the scope that created it.

evals/promptfoo/providers/output_organizer_provider.py — D2 patch 3.

output_organizer needs its OWN provider, separate from role_provider.py.
Traced agents/output_organizer.py directly rather than assuming it fit
role_provider.py's shape, and it doesn't, on two counts:

  1. Not Role-Library-driven at all. It has no ROLE_PROMPTS_SEED entry
     and no eo.registry.REGISTRY entry -- it's called directly from
     api/task_runner.py, outside the resolve()/generic_worker dispatch
     system entirely. Its SYSTEM_PROMPT and CHAIN are hardcoded module
     constants (own docstring: "Deliberately its own module rather than
     a generic_worker role"). get_role_prompt() has nothing to fetch for
     it -- role_provider.py's _reject_real_action_role() guard (patch
     2b) wouldn't even catch this case, since it only checks
     eo.registry.REGISTRY, and output_organizer isn't in there either.
  2. Different calling shape. Every role_provider.py case is
     (role_name, task_text) -> str. organize_final_answer() takes the
     WHOLE finished role_outputs tree (role_name -> raw_output) plus the
     original user_request, and returns a structured
     {"answer": str, "dedup_notes": dict}, not a bare string.

So rather than bend role_provider.py to fit a second, incompatible
shape, this is its own file with its own promptfoo config
(output_organizer.promptfooconfig.yaml) -- same "separate, not
shoehorned into the main config" pattern patch 5's provider-comparison
config already uses f

relay/emitter.py — Stage 6, step 1 of the roadmap (Part 10):
    "Stand up the Pusher app (free tier), wire the event-emitting wrapper
    into one agent first (e.g. the Inspector) as a proof of concept."

    session_id=None params to existing agents without changing their
    behavior for every caller that doesn't pass one yet (CLI usage,

scripts/backfill_chat_messages.py — Perf audit item #1, step 1.2.

Copies every chat's existing `chats.messages` JSONB array into the new
`chat_messages` table (migrations/0002_add_chat_messages_table.sql),
one row per message, preserving array order via `seq`.

This script ONLY reads chats.messages and writes chat_messages — it
never touches or clears the old JSONB column. Safe to re-run: each
chat is skipped if chat_messages already has a row count matching that
chat's current messages array length, so a second run after new
messages have arrived (via the still-unchanged append_message()) will
correctly backfill only what's missing. It does NOT attempt to merge
or diff individual messages within a partially-backfilled chat -- if
the counts don't match, the chat's existing chat_messages rows for
that chat are deleted and it's backfilled from scratch, since `seq`
must exactly mirror array order and a partial/interleaved backfill
would be worse than redoing it.

This is intentionally NOT run automatically anywhere -- append_message()
and get_chat() are NOT changed by this step (that's step 1.3). Until
that step lands, chat_messages is a shadow copy only; the JSONB column
in chats remains the sole source of truth the app actually reads from.

Usage (PowerShell):
    python scripts/backfill_chat_messages.py            # do the backfill
    python scripts/backfill_chat_messages.py --dry-run   # report counts only, write nothing

with a recorder at every place content could come to rest.

WHAT IS REAL AND WHAT IS FAKE
-----------------------------
Real, on the server: the device socket (codeagent/ws.py) served by uvicorn on 127.0.0.1, the message router, the run
handlers, the emitter, the tool broker, the agent loop (codeagent/loop.py) wired in by codeagent/wiring.py as
api/server.py wires it, the budgeted context assembler, metering, the run manager, the run store (see MODES) and the
encrypted run buffer (codeagent/buffer.py: real AES-GCM, real key derivation).

Real, on the device: the genuine C04 DeviceLink over a genuine TCP WebSocket, the tool runner, the policy engine, the
file and shell tools (real `bash` on a temporary project), checkpoints, the instruction loader (M2C.md goes into
run.start), the local SQLite store, and the terminal chat's session controller (m2c/tui/session.py) with a fake screen.

Fake: the model (loop_testkit.ScriptedAdapter: it streams text and proposes tool calls from a script), Redis (the repo's
in-memory twins, each wrapped so that every command is recorded), the person (an auto-approver of the approval prompts)
and, in fake mode only, Postgres (see MODES).

backend/tests/canary/scanners.py -- Patch Q06: the scanners behind the "no content at rest" canary test.

WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
--------------------
The trust statement of the product (build plan section O1, 11.3, 11.4) is that the server keeps no prompt, no file
content, no path, no command and no tool output once a run is over, and never writes any of them to Postgres, to a
log, to an error report or to a metric.  A test of that statement is only worth something if a green result cannot be
produced by a scanner that looks in the wrong place or for the wrong shape.  So this module has two halves, and the
tests in this package use both:

  * the NEEDLES: for every planted canary, every form it commonly takes when it passes through a serializer (raw, the
    random token alone, JSON-escaped, JSON-in-JSON, URL-encoded, base64 and base64url at all three byte alignments,
    hex, Python escapes, UTF-16), the two halves of the random token (what is left when a canary is cut in two by a line
    break or a log prefix) and a "squashed" form that survives being wrapped;
  * the SCANNERS: one per place content could come to rest (Postgres rows, every SQL statement and parameter that a
    recording fake saw, application logs, Redis keys and values, error-reporting payloads, the usage ledger, and the
    device's own store, which is ALLOWED to hold content).  Each takes the thing to look at and returns hits; nothing in
    here asserts by itself, `assert_clean` does.

backend/tests/canary/test_no_content_at_rest.py -- Patch Q06: the "no content at rest" canary test.

This is the test that backs the product's trust statement (build plan O1): the server keeps no prompt, no file content,
no path, no command and no tool output once a run is over, writes none of them to Postgres, to a log, to an error
report or to a metric, and while a run is open keeps its content only in the encrypted run buffer.

HOW IT WORKS (details in harness.py and README.md next to it)
-------------------------------------------------------------
Every scenario plants fresh random canaries in the prompt, in the project's files, in tool output, in the model's reply,
in tool arguments (a path and a command), and in an instruction file (M2C.md, loaded into run.start).  It then runs one
scripted session end to end in this process: the real server code over a real WebSocket, the real device code in a
temporary project, a recorder at every storage place, the real logging configuration, and the error-reporting SDK
initialised with a transport that keeps what it would send.  Then every place content could rest is scanned for every
canary in every common encoded form (scanners.py).  A hit anywhere fails the test.

The scenarios: a normal finish (and `completed`), a cancel in the middle of a model answer, a disconnect during a tool
call and the resume, a failure of the model, a tool error, a quota pause, and a ledger failure (metering fails open).
A separate test forces error rep

functions.doc1: Nothing the server may not keep, in any place it could keep it.

functions.name: check_after_end
functions.doc1: Nothing may remain in Redis for a run in a terminal state (`allow_prefix`: the one documented exception, which has its own strict xfail; a leftover key of any other name still fails here).

backend/tests/canary/test_scanner_selftest.py -- Patch Q06: proof that a green canary result cannot come from a scanner
that looks in the wrong place.

test_no_content_at_rest.py scans nine kinds of place.  Here a canary is planted, on purpose, in EACH of them:

  * through the real recorders of the harness wherever one exists (a log record on the server's loggers, a Redis
    command on the run buffer's twin and on run_guard's, a SQL statement or store call, an error report captured by
    the real SDK, a row in a real Postgres table when a database URL is set, a row in the device's SQLite store), and
  * through the Result record that the checks read, field by field (so a field that stopped being checked is caught).

and the matching check must fail, naming the place.  It is then repeated for every encoded form that commonly slips
through (JSON-escaped, JSON in JSON, URL-encoded, base64 and base64url at all three alignments, hex, Python escapes) and
for a canary split across two log lines or two Redis values.  Finally a CLEAN run must pass the same checks, so the
checks are not simply always failing.

Everything is made at run time (gitleaks): canaries are random strings, never literals.

files.module_doc:
Shared fixtures for the whole tests/ tree (unit + integration).

Two problems this file exists to solve, both found during the B1 audit:

1. Several old test/dev scripts call memory.bus functions directly, which
   hit your REAL Upstash Redis (memory/bus.py's module-level `redis`
   client). At LEAST test_brief_writer.py, test_staff_task_e2e.py,
   test_seed_bootstrap.py, test_memory_bus.py, test_namespacing.py, and
   test_planner.py do this — one of them (test_seed_bootstrap.py) calls
   write(ROLE_PROMPTS_KEY, None), which wipes your real role-prompt
   registry if run against production Redis.

   Fix: `memory.bus` only ever touches Redis through the single
   module-level `redis` object (get/set/delete/mget — confirmed by
   auditing memory/bus.py directly). This autouse fixture swaps that one
   object for an in-memory FakeRedis before every test and restores it
   after, so nothing under tests/ can ever touch production data, with
   zero per-test-file changes required.

2. Most agents import `generate_text` directly into their own module
   namespace (`from utils.llm_client import generate_text`), so
   `unittest.mock.patch("utils.llm_client.generate_text")` does NOT mock
   the copy an agent actually calls — you have to patch it in every
   agent module individually, which is exactly the kind of thing that
   silently rots as new agents get added. `patch_generate_text()` below
   patches every module currently holding a bound reference to it, found
   by walking sys.

tests/integration/hello_testkit.py -- Patch I01: the harness for the walking-skeleton tests.

One `Stack` joins the real pieces and fakes only what sits at a module boundary:

    real    codeagent.ws (S04) + router + run_handlers (S14) + emitter + hello (I01)
            run_manager / runs / buffer (S06) over their in-memory twins (World)
            the S05 adapter, talking HTTP to S05's own FakeProvider
            eo.credits (S02)
            m2c.link.DeviceLink (C04), m2c.repl (I01), the m2c local store (C02)
    fake    the database calls: devices (Rig's WsFakeStore), runs (FakeRunStore),
            the usage ledger (FakeLedger below), Redis (FakeRunRedis)

The device socket is served by uvicorn on 127.0.0.1 in a thread, so the genuine C04 client uses a
genuine TCP WebSocket (handshake, frames, abrupt connection loss). The client's source is
imported from the repo (m2c/src) because the backend's CI job does not pip-install m2c; its only
third-party dependency, `websockets`, is in the backend requirements.

Fake secrets are built at run time (gitleaks flags anything shaped like a key).

is eo/panel.py's _get_or_write_role_prompt(), which every tab in the

Three layers, cheapest/most-deterministic first:

1. Schema validation (`_validate`) — pure unit tests, no network, always run.
2. Fallback-chain engagement — mocks the provider clients so a "bad key on
   the primary" scenario is reproducible without needing an actually-bad

   against real providers. Skipped automatically if EO_INSPECTOR_GROQ_KEY_1
   isn't set, since these need real credentials and real network access,
   and their point is calibrating against real model behavior, not CI
   hygiene. Run these yourself once your .env has real keys:

    python -m pytest tests/integration/test_eo_inspector.py -v -s

Real-Postgres checks for S06c (codeagent/run_manager.py).

The unit tests (tests/unit/test_codeagent_run_manager.py) use an in-memory twin of the run
store. This file runs the manager against the REAL `runs` table (migration 0014), so what
only Postgres can prove is proved here:

  * the sweep's one cross-account READ: the SQL of PgSweepStore, through the trusted
    internal path, returns only open, idle runs, in (updated_at, id) order, keyset-paged,
    and only ids and timestamps; a cursor with an acting user (not trusted) does not see
    other accounts' runs, so the sweep really does depend on that path;

Patch M2C-Q06b: the `canary` job installs the backend and the m2c client in two steps, and checks the result.

The problem this guards against. backend/requirements.txt pins ``rich==14.3.4`` (guardrails-ai 0.10.2 needs rich below 15,
e2b needs 14 or newer) while m2c/pyproject.toml pins ``rich==15.0.0`` and ``prompt_toolkit==3.0.53`` for the terminal UI.
``pip install -r requirements.txt -e ../m2c`` therefore ends in ``ResolutionImpossible``, and the `canary` job failed at
its first install step. The canary test never imports the terminal UI (only ``m2c/tui/app.py`` imports those two
libraries, and the harness imports ``m2c.tui.session``, which does not), and ``websockets`` is pinned to the same
version in both packages, so the job installs the backend first and then ``pip install --no-deps -e ../m2c``.

What this file checks, with no network and no pip run:

1. ci.yml parses, and the canary job installs in two steps: the backend requirements in one command that does not
   mention m2c, and ``--no-deps -e ../m2c`` (no ``[dev]`` extra) in a later one. No job anywhere puts the backend
   requirements and m2c on one pip command line.
2. A ``pip check`` step comes after both installs and before the first pytest step. ``--no-deps`` leaves m2c's own
   ``rich==15.0.0`` and ``prompt_toolkit`` requirements unmet on purpose, so a plain ``pip check`` would always fail:
   the step tolerates exactly those two lines and fails on anything else (a drifted ``websockets``, a new m2c runtime

tests/static/test_event_type_coverage.py — PATCH-D: the drift guard.

PATCH-A introduced relay/emitter.py's EventType enum as the single
source of truth for event types, and PATCH-B repointed eo/notify.py's
VALID_KINDS at a curated subset of it (NOTIFY_KINDS), closing the two
places this codebase's event-type allowlist used to drift out of sync
with its own call sites. PATCH-C made an unrecognized type degrade
(logged + skipped) instead of raising, so that drift can no longer
crash a task run in production.

None of that stops drift from *happening* again -- it just stops it
from being catastrophic when it does. A call site can still pass a
plain string literal (nothing enforces "always use EventType.X"), and
if that literal is never added to EventType, the event just silently
never gets sent -- which is much better than crashing the run, but is
still a real, findable bug that's better caught at CI time than
discovered later by "huh, why did this notification/diagram/deploy
status never show up on the frontend."

agents/, eo/, and relay/ and asserts every string literal passed as an
event_type / kind argument to emit_event(), emit_user_event(), or
notify() resolves to a real EventType / NOTIFY_KINDS member. It does
NOT flag calls that already pass EventType.X directly (an Attribute
node, not a string Constant) -- those are already statically safe:
a typo there is an AttributeError at import time, long before th

S04b: the device socket's runtime needs are provided by every deployment path.

backend/codeagent/ws.py validates every message with protocol/validate.py, which needs

  * jsonschema (with `referencing`, `jsonschema-specifications` and `rpds-py`), and
  * the protocol/ directory itself (protocol/v1/*.json), found by
    codeagent.ws.load_protocol() at <backend>/protocol or <repo root>/protocol.

Without either, load_protocol() raises ProtocolUnavailable and the socket fails closed
(`internal`, close 1011) -- safe, but the feature would be dead on arrival in a container.
This file reads the deployment files as TEXT, so it holds where Docker and pip are not
available, and fails on exactly the three ways that regression can come back:

  1. the pins the two requirements files share drift apart (protocol/requirements.txt is
     what the `protocol` CI job installs, backend/requirements.txt is what ships; a
     version that differs between them means the contract is tested against one
     jsonschema and served by another);
  2. backend.Dockerfile stops copying protocol/ to /app/protocol (the image's layout:
     WORKDIR /app holds backend/, so <backend>/protocol is /app/protocol);
  3. docker-compose.dev.yml stops mounting ./protocol at /app/protocol (its
     `./backend:/app` bind mount hides everything the image copied under /app, so the
     directory has to be mounted back in; read-only because nothing writes there).

(migration 0003), and later migrations narrow what that role may do to
individual tables. Migration 0009 grants `SELECT, INSERT, DELETE` on

The run manager glues three things that already have in-memory twins, so this file only
adds the missing pieces and ties them together:

  World             one object holding every stand-in, with ONE clock for all of them:
                      store     runs_testkit.FakeRunStore    (the `runs` table)
                      sweep     FakeSweepStore               (the cross-account read)
                      redis     buffer_testkit.FakeRunRedis  (the run buffer)
                      guard     FakeGuardRedis               (eo/run_guard's keys)
                    advance(seconds) moves all clocks together; `now` is the same
                    instant as a datetime.
  FakeGuardRedis    the few commands eo/run_guard uses (get/set/delete/incr/incrby/
                    expire), in memory, so a test can assert that nothing is left.
  FakeSweepStore    codeagent.run_manager.PgSweepStore over the FakeRunStore's rows:
                    open runs idle since before a cutoff, keyset-paged on (updated_at, id).
  start_payload()   a run.start payload that is valid against protocol/v1.

files.module_doc:
Shared fakes for the S06 run-manager tests (not collected: no test_ prefix).

  Clock          a controllable clock, so timestamps can be told apart without
                 sleeping.
  FakeRunStore   an in-memory codeagent.runs.PgRunStore with the same atomic
                 semantics: one lock makes every method atomic, like a single SQL
                 statement; `move` only succeeds if the row is still in the state
                 the caller read (the conditional UPDATE); the parallel-run cap is
                 counted inside the same critical section as the insert / resume
                 (the advisory lock). It also enforces the two things the
                 migration's trigger enforces, so a test that tries to cheat the
                 state machine through the store fails the way the database would:
                 a terminal row never changes state, and counters never decrease.
                 The SQL itself, the trigger and the policies are covered by
                 tests/integration/test_runs_pg.py.

                 Two hooks make races deterministic instead of lucky:
                   after_get(user_id, run_id, row)   called after every `get`, outside
                                                     the lock -- put a barrier here so
                                                     every racer has READ before any
                                                     of them WRITES;
                   before_move(call)                 called at

tests/unit/test_agent_correction_locator.py — Patch 7f-3.

Covers agents/correction_locator.py's locate_correction(): turning a
plain-language correction into a located, proposed JSON Patch
"replace" op against Secondary Data -- never touching Primary Source.
Two-pass posture (module docstring §8b):

  1. No candidate topics in scope -> short-circuit, no LLM call.
  2. _parse_decision(): degrade-don't-break on malformed/missing JSON;
     out-of-scope topic_id dropped; edit fields outside
     _EDITABLE_FIELDS dropped; non-string edit values dropped.
  3. Pass-1-only path: summary alone was enough (needs_source=False,
     edit present) -> _build_op() called directly, no second LLM call.
  4. Pass-2 fallback: pass 1 asks for source, or comes back with no
     usable edit -> real excerpt pulled and a second call made; no
     excerpt available -> gives up with a reason; second pass with no
     edit -> gives up with a reason.
  5. _build_op(): only the edited fields change; a vanished topic
     (concurrent delete) returns None, surfaced as "topic no longer
     exists".
  6. _candidate_topics(): scope_node_ids=None means every topic;
     otherwise only topics whose `covers` intersects scope_node_ids.

dispatch (which is how this module is actually invoked) has no
special-case handling for it either, so a raised JSONDecodeError here
propagates as an ordinary agent-step failure through the same path any
other unhandled exception from an UNSCOPED_TIER_AGENTS callable would --
not a silent data-quality problem. This suite pins that behavior down as
a regression guard (it raises, it doesn't swallow) rather than treating
it as a bug to patch over.

The bug these pin: an UNHANDLED exception (a DB error, any bug) used to
be answered by Starlette's outermost ServerErrorMiddleware, i.e. from
outside CORSMiddleware, so the 500 carried no Access-Control-Allow-Origin
header and the browser surfaced it as an opaque "Failed to fetch"

the exact function api/server.py calls — rather than importing
api.server (which boots the DB pool, Sentry, Laya, MCP...), so the real
middleware order is what's under test.

S09: the server tool broker (codeagent/broker.py).

The broker proposes a tool call to the connected device (tool_proposed, a stream message) and
waits for the device's answer: a tool_result if it ran the tool, an approval{deny} if its policy
refused. It never numbers anything (the `emit` it is given does), never decides an approval,
and keeps its state in memory behind a small interface (S11 moves it to shared storage).

These tests use a RECORDING FAKE for `emit` (what the loop, S07, will pass: RunEmitter.emit)
and a fake connection registry, so they need neither the run store, the buffer nor jsonschema.
tests/unit/test_codeagent_broker_wiring.py runs the same broker behind the real S14 handlers,
emitter and run store, and checks every frame against protocol/v1.

  * propose, the matching tool_result, the trust label ........................ test_propose_*, test_trust_*
  * timeout: `error` tool_timeout + tool_finished timeout ...................... test_timeout_*
  * duplicate results: first wins, counted; late results ignored ............... test_duplicate_*, test_late_*
  * idempotent re-proposal (no second tool_proposed) ........................... test_reproposal_*
  * cross-run / cross-device / cross-user injection is rejected ................. test_foreign_*
  * disconnect during a call (tool_finished disconnected, waiters released) ..... test_disconnect_*

Patch L01a: the model-facing catalog now holds ``ask_user`` and ``tasks``.

The server runs neither tool: it forwards them to the device like any other (S09's broker) and the person's
answer comes back as an ordinary ``tool_result``.  So the only thing the backend can check is the CATALOG: the
two definitions load, are R0 (visible in plan mode), validate model input the way the schema says and are
offered to the provider with their descriptions.  Nothing here touches a database or a network.

Patch S07b -- unit tests for leaving plan mode (codeagent/loop.py and runs.set_mode).

THE GAP THESE TESTS PIN. A run's mode reaches the server once, in run.start. In plan mode the loop shows the model
only the read-only tools plus plan_exit. When the person approves plan_exit the DEVICE leaves plan mode and answers
the call with a successful tool_result; the server was never told, so the model stayed read-only for the rest of the
run. S07b makes the loop switch the run to `ask` when (and only when) an OK plan_exit comes back for a run that is in
plan mode, and STORE the new mode in the run row (the buffer's state is sealed once, so a resume reads the row).

Groups: runs.set_mode itself (over the in-memory run store), the switch inside a turn, every case that must leave
the mode alone, the switch surviving a resume, and the log. The run, its buffer, run_manager and run_guard are the
REAL S06 modules over their in-memory twins (the same Rig the S07 tests use); the model is scripted and the broker
is a recording fake.

Patch S15 -- the loop's one additive change: tools are offered only to a connection that can answer them.

The device says what it can do in `hello.capabilities`; the server keeps that on the connection. S15's wiring
gives the loop a small predicate (`offer_tools(conn) -> bool`); the loop asks it once per turn and, when the answer
is no, offers NO tools to the model and refuses any call the model makes anyway, so that a `tool_proposed` is never
sent to a client that cannot answer it. These tests drive the loop alone (the scripted model, the real S06
modules over their in-memory twins, a recording broker); tests/unit/test_codeagent_wiring_flow.py drives the same
rule through the real router, run handlers and broker.

  * no predicate (the default): exactly what S07 did, every visible tool is offered ........ test_default_*
  * predicate says no: no tools in the request, the reply still streams .................... test_no_tools_*
  * a call the model makes anyway: never forwarded, answered with a fixed text ............ test_a_call_*
  * the predicate is given the turn's connection and asked once per turn ................... test_predicate_*
  * a predicate that raises: no tools (fail closed), the type is logged, never the text ..... test_a_failing_*
  * plan mode and the gate compose: the gate can only remove tools, never widen them ....... test_plan_mode_*

S04b: in a backend install, the device socket's protocol reader loads.

codeagent/ws.py validates every message with protocol/validate.py, which needs
jsonschema (and `referencing`) and the protocol/v1 schemas. Until S04b a backend
install only got jsonschema transitively (guardrails-ai, litellm) and the container
had no protocol/ directory, so load_protocol() raised ProtocolUnavailable there and the
socket failed closed.

This file is the other half of tests/static/test_protocol_runtime.py (which reads the
requirements files, the Dockerfile and the dev overlay as text): it proves that in the
environment `pip install -r backend/requirements.txt` builds, the production loader
really works. It is deliberately NOT guarded by pytest.importorskip("jsonschema"): a
backend install that lacks jsonschema is exactly the regression to catch, so it must
fail here rather than skip. It lives in tests/unit because CI's backend job runs
`pytest tests/unit tests/integration` and does not collect tests/static.

The image and the dev overlay are checked by hand with the commands in the S04b patch
description (docker build, then `python -c "from codeagent.ws import load_protocol; ..."`).

Everything runs against in-memory twins behind the real interfaces (see
tests/unit/run_manager_testkit.py): the run store, the sweep read, the Redis buffer and
eo/run_guard's Redis, all on one clock, so an idle expiry or the 24 h cap is crossed

Regression coverage for two bugs found by tracing eo/concurrency_gate.py's
outer per-account throttle against the CURRENT utils/rate_ledger.py:

  1. _admit() always reserved 1 unit with no max_output_tokens, regardless
     of gating mode. Harmless for "tokens"/"requests" (a deliberate
     placeholder there -- see _outer_reservation_size()'s docstring), but
     in "neurons" mode that "1" is interpreted as a 1-token input
     estimate with no output ceiling, so _estimate_neurons() always
     returned a fraction-of-a-neuron figure -- reserve() could never
     actually refuse admission for a Cloudflare account, no matter how
     exhausted its real daily neuron budget was.

  2. The cancelled-future rollback path in _run_one() called
     rate_ledger.release_reservation(reservation_id) with no other args,
     relying on that meaning "full rollback". release_reservation()'s
     current signature defaults dispatched=True (settle), so that call
     was silently settling instead of rolling back -- a cancelled task's
     outer reservation stayed permanently booked.

autouse fake_bus fixture (tests/conftest.py) so these tests exercise the
actual reserve()/release_reservation()/_gating_mode_for() code, the same
