eo/audit_log.py had zero test coverage before this. The one hard
guarantee this module makes -- write_audit() NEVER raises, even on a

actual operation it's describing" -- is exactly the kind of contract

     must not become findings about the user's code.

sanitize_parallel_groups()'s six independent safety checks (see that

check could still pass the integration scenario if the others happen to

(pre-existing nested-group entries, and "nothing survived") that a

was never staffed for, run something mid-way through a human-approval
checkpoint, or run the same role twice concurrently. Malformed/
adversarial input must always degrade to the flat, sequential order --
never raise, never silently do something unsafe -- so every test below
asserts the SAFE outcome, not just "no exception."

tier-3 (whole-project) layer of the three-tier memory model, and the
highest-value things to pin down are:

    addressed by a stable `candidate_id`, not list position, because
    two reviewers can be looking at the same pending list at once.

    must succeed even if cache invalidation itself blows up.

tests/unit/test_eo_ws_registry.py — Patch 7e-2.

eo/ws_registry.py had zero test coverage before this. This is the
bridge that lets notify() -- called synchronously from deep inside
sync agent code running on FastAPI's threadpool, not the event loop
-- actually reach a live WebSocket. A bug here either drops real-time
UI updates silently (push() swallowing everything when it shouldn't)
or crashes the calling agent code (an unguarded broadcast failure
propagating back through notify()'s call site, which the module's own
_broadcast() docstring says must never happen).

Isolation: _connections and _loop are plain module-level globals, not
something ws_registry.py exposes a reset for -- an autouse fixture in
this file resets both before every test so state from one test can't
leak into the next (same class of leak tests/conftest.py's own
_reset_role_prompts_cache/_reset_app_slug_context fixtures guard
against for other modules).

_broadcast() is a coroutine, scheduled via a real running event loop
(asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe) -- tests that exercise it directly
use @pytest.mark.anyio, matching the pattern tests/unit/
test_eo_local_workspace.py already establishes for testing async eo/
code in this repo (its own local `anyio_backend` fixture, reused here
rather than invented fresh).

files.module_doc:
utils/error_sanitizer.py -- Reliability & Smart Rate-Limiting Overhaul,
Patch I.1 (REVISED Phase I).

Problem this closes: raw provider exceptions (Groq/Cerebras/OpenAI
`APIStatusError` bodies, Cloudflare REST error text, etc.) were being
f-string-interpolated straight into `emit_event("error", ...)` payloads
and API response `message` fields -- both of which are read directly by
the frontend chat bubble / API caller. Those bodies can carry things
like the provider org ID, a billing/console URL, or a verbatim
`Error code: ...` blob that has no business leaving the server.

This module is the one place that turns "some exception" into "a short,
safe, user-facing string." It never changes what gets logged -- callers
keep doing `traceback.print_exc()` / Sentry breadcrumbs / etc. exactly
as before; this only changes what goes out over the wire.

Classification reuses `llm_errors.classify_error()` when the exception
looks like an LLM-provider error (i.e. `classify_error` doesn't have to
guess blind -- it already knows how to read a provider body), so a
RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW failure reads differently to the user than a
PERMANENT_AUTH one. Anything that isn't recognizable as a provider error
at all (a bare KeyError from application code, for instance) falls back
to one generic message -- we don't try to classify non-provider
exceptions, we just decline to repeat their text.

functions.name: user_facing_message
functions.doc1: Return a short, safe, generic string describing `exc`, suitable for a chat bubble or an API response body.

utils/llm_client.py — replaces utils/gemini_client.py entirely.

OpenRouter is not used anywhere in this system (per the v5 Master
Blueprint correction). GitHub Models was used here too until its full
retirement on 2026-07-30 (quota-reality fix, §4) -- every chain that
stepped through it has since been moved onto a different provider or had
that step removed outright; nothing in this module routes to it anymore.
This module provides one generic generate_text() function that any agent
can call with its own ordered fallback chain, drawn from: Groq,
Mistral, Gemini, HuggingFace, Cloudflare Workers AI.

Each agent defines its own chain as a list of steps. Most providers
(groq, openrouter, mistral, gemini, huggingface) are OpenAI-SDK-shaped
and use "key_env":

    CHAIN = [
        {"provider": "groq", "model": "openai/gpt-oss-120b", "key_env": "GROQ_API_KEY"},
        {"provider": "groq", "model": "qwen/qwen3.6-27b", "key_env": "GROQ_API_KEY"},
        {"provider": "openrouter", "model": "openrouter/free", "key_env": "OPENROUTER_API_KEY_9"},
    ]

Cloudflare Workers AI is a plain REST call needing two credentials, so
its step shape is different -- "account_id_env" and "token_env" instead
of a single "key_env":

    CHAIN = [
        {"provider": "cloudflare", "model": "@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast",
         "account_id_env": "CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID_4", "token_env": "CLOUDFLARE_API_KEY_4"},
    ]

generate_text() walks the chain in order, moving to the next step only

utils/llm_errors.py -- Reliability & Smart Rate-Limiting Overhaul, Phase 1
(error taxonomy). Foundation module: every later phase (the rate ledger,
proactive gating, bounded concurrency, quota-aware chain construction,
graceful degradation, scoped chunking, observability, the final
exhaustive-wait tier) dispatches on the ErrorBucket this module returns,
so this is the one place that decides what kind of failure just happened.

This replaces llm_client.py's current single-signal
`_is_request_too_large_error()` (status_code == 413 or "request too
large" in the message) branching. That check conflated two genuinely
different failures: a request that is actually too large for a model's
context window, and Groq's rolling per-minute TPM quota (also surfaced
as a 413) being temporarily exhausted for the organization. The log that
motivated this plan showed a 229-character prompt shrunk twice and still
failing -- proof the old check was misclassifying an org-scoped,
time-windowed quota problem as a per-request size problem. classify_error()
below reads the provider's own wording first, and only falls back to a
bare status-code guess when the body doesn't say.

Recovery table (the contract every downstream phase must respect):

    CONTEXT_LENGTH_EXCEEDED -> trim/chunk *this* request only (scoped
        chunking, Phase 7). Never retry unchanged on the next provider --
        an unchanged oversized request fails identically everywhere.
    RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW -> check the rate ledger (

utils/mermaid_lint.py — rendering audit fix.

agents/mind_mapper.py and agents/workflow_suggester.py both extract a
```mermaid fenced block from an LLM's answer with nothing stronger than
"does the fence exist" (see each file's own _MERMAID_BLOCK_RE). Neither
module validates what's actually *inside* the fence, and both say so
explicitly in their docstrings/comments -- a real Mermaid syntax error
"isn't something regex validation can catch anyway." That's true for a
full grammar-level check (this repo has no Mermaid parser available on
the Python side, and standing one up via a Node subprocess for a
best-effort lint is a lot of moving parts for what's ultimately a
best-effort check), but it understates what a *heuristic* check can
still catch cheaply: empty content, a missing/unrecognized diagram-type
header, unbalanced brackets/quotes, and a flowchart/graph with no edges
at all are all common, cheap-to-detect ways an LLM's Mermaid answer
comes back broken -- and they're exactly the kind of thing that was
previously sailing straight through to MermaidDiagram.jsx, which would
then hit mermaid.render()'s reject path and show the user a "couldn't
render this diagram" fallback with no server-side retry ever having been
attempted.

This is intentionally NOT a full parser. It can have false negatives
(a diagram that passes here can still fail to render -- e.g. a typo'd
node shape or an unknown arrow variant) and, much more rarely, false
positives are avoided by keeping every check

daemon/connection.py — F2 Part 2 + Part 3: the daemon's outbound
WebSocket client. Part 2 built connect/hello/hello_ack/reconnect;
Part 3 adds actual handling for the one message type that can arrive
on this connection now -- {"type": "tool_call", ...} -- dispatching it
to daemon/tools.py and sending the {"type": "tool_result", ...} back.
See eo/local_workspace.py's docstring (backend side) for the full wire
shape both halves of this protocol agree on.

nothing here beyond new entries in daemon/tools.py's dispatch table.

Part 7 adds one real change: execute_command now streams. Instead of
always going through tools.dispatch() and waiting for one final
result, _handle_tool_call() special-cases "execute_command" to call
tools.execute_command() directly with an `on_chunk` callback that
sends a `{"type": "tool_stream", ...}` message for every line of
output as the subprocess produces it -- see tools.execute_command's
own docstring for why that callback runs on a reader thread, not this
module's event loop, and _send_stream_chunk_threadsafe below for how a
thread-called callback safely gets a message onto this asyncio
websocket connection. Every other tool (list_dir/read_file/write_file/
delete) is completely unaffected: dispatch() is called for those
exactly as it was in Part 3/4, one call in, one tool_result out.

daemon/path_guard.py — F2 Part 1: the one function every later part
(read tool calls in Part 3, write/delete/execute in Part 4) must route
every filesystem path through before touching disk.

Why this is its own module rather than a method on the daemon class:
Part 3 and Part 4 both need it, and it has to be trivially unit-testable
in isolation from any websocket/event-loop code, since a bug here is a
containment-boundary bug, not a feature bug.

The check is deliberately conservative:
- Resolves symlinks (`Path.resolve()`), so a symlink inside the allowed
  root that points outside it is rejected, not followed.
- Rejects the allowed root itself being (or resolving to) `/`, the
  daemon's own install directory, or the user's home directory root --
  configuring the daemon with an overly broad root is a setup mistake
  this module can catch even though it can't stop the user from doing
  it deliberately.
- Uses `os.path.commonpath`, not a plain string-prefix check, so
  `/home/user/project-x` is never treated as "inside"
  `/home/user/project` just because the string happens to start with
  it.

Place this file at: daemon/path_guard.py

127.0.0.1:<MINIME_PREVIEW_PORT> in front of the person's own dev server
(MINIME_PREVIEW_TARGET, e.g. http://localhost:5173). Pasting the
proxy's address into the workbench's "Dev server URL" box (W7.3) then
gives them, with no change to their app:

     CSP `frame-ancestors` refuse to render inside the preview iframe;

     the frontend's /mm-inspector.js route) is injected into HTML
     *document* responses, so hover/click selection works. Mapping a
     clicked element to a source line still needs the build-time plugin

m2c/src/m2c/__init__.py -- Patch C01: the M2C client package.

``m2c`` is the local half of M2C (Minime to Code): a Python command-line
client that will, in later work packages, store sessions on this machine
(C02), sign in with a device code (C03), keep a link to the MiniMe server
(C04) and execute tools locally (C05+).  This first patch (C01) is only the
skeleton: the package layout, the ``m2c`` console entry point, the config
directory, a content-free logging setup and a minimal ``m2c doctor``.

Design rules that every later patch inherits (build plan §0.2 and §1):

* Python >= 3.11 (decision D1) and the standard library only at runtime
  until a work package explicitly adds a dependency.  tests/test_cli.py
  enforces this.
* Security checks fail closed; telemetry and logging fail open.
* Nothing the user typed, the model produced or a tool returned is ever
  written to a log (see logging_setup.py).
* Everything the client keeps on disk lives under one directory, ``~/.m2c``
  by default, relocatable with the ``M2C_HOME`` environment variable so that
  tests never touch the real home directory.

This module deliberately imports nothing, so ``import m2c`` is free and the
version can be read by the build backend without importing the package.

Place this file at: m2c/src/m2c/__init__.py

m2c/src/m2c/auth/__init__.py -- Patch C03: signing in, and the credential.

    login.py         ``m2c login`` (the device-code flow), ``m2c logout`` and
                     ``get_access_token()``
    credentials.py   the stored device credential (OS keyring or a 0600 file),
                     the redacting ``Secret``/``Credential`` types and every
                     exception this package raises

What other work packages use:

* C04 (device link) calls ``load_credential()`` and sends the credential in the
  socket's ``hello`` message (P00 authenticates the socket with the credential
  itself; there is no JWT on it).
* Later HTTP calls call ``get_access_token()``.  Nothing in Wave 2 or 3 needs it
  yet.

Importing this package imports neither ``keyring`` nor anything outside the
standard library; the keyring is loaded lazily, only when a credential is
saved, read or deleted, and is never required.

``login`` the function is deliberately NOT re-exported here: ``m2c.auth.login``
is the module, and a function of the same name would shadow it.  Call
``m2c.auth.login.login(...)``.

Place this file at: m2c/src/m2c/auth/__init__.py

m2c/src/m2c/auth/credentials.py -- Patch C03: the device credential, where it
is kept on this machine, and the error types of the whole ``auth`` package.

WHAT A DEVICE CREDENTIAL IS
---------------------------
``m2c login`` (login.py) ends with the server handing this device one long
random string, exactly once (S03, backend/eo/devices.py: 256 random bits, only
its SHA-256 is stored server side).  That string is the thing that
authenticates the device from then on:

* ``get_access_token()`` (login.py) exchanges it for a ~15 minute JWT for
  plain HTTP calls;
* C04's device link sends it in the socket's ``hello`` message
  (protocol/v1/hello.json ``device_credential``), because P00 authenticates
  the socket with the credential itself and there is no JWT on it.  C04 reads
  it with ``load_credential()`` below.

Besides the secret, the record carries the ``device_id`` the server assigned
and the ``server_url`` that issued it.  The URL matters: a credential must only
ever be sent to the server that issued it (see ``ServerMismatchError`` in
login.py), so it is stored with the credential rather than trusted from the
environment at the moment of use.

WHERE IT IS KEPT
----------------
1. The OS keyring, when the optional ``keyring`` package is installed
   (``pip install 'm2c[keyring]'``) AND it has a usable backend.  The module is
   imported lazily and is never required; keyring's own "fail" backend, which
   is what a stock WSL2 install ends up with (build plan §11.1: Secret Se

m2c/src/m2c/auth/login.py -- Patch C03: ``m2c login``, ``m2c logout`` and the
access-token helper.

THE FLOW (OAuth device authorisation, RFC 8628; server side is S03,
backend/api/routes/devices.py and backend/eo/devices.py -- these are the exact
shapes this module talks to)::

    login(server_url)
      POST /v1/code/devices/pair/start  {device_name, os, client_version}
        -> {device_code (secret), user_code, verification_url, interval, expires_in}
      print user_code and verification_url        (never opens a browser)
      every `interval` seconds:
        POST /v1/code/devices/pair/poll {device_code}
          -> {status: pending}                     keep waiting
             {status: approved, device_credential, device_id}   (ONCE)
             {status: denied} | {status: expired}  stop, say so
      store the credential (credentials.py), tell the person where

    get_access_token()
      POST /v1/code/devices/token {device_credential} -> {jwt, expires_in}
      cached in memory, refreshed before it expires

No browser is launched: from WSL2, and from any ssh session, that usually
fails, and the page works from any device anyway (build plan §11.1).

PATIENCE AND LIMITS
-------------------
* The server's ``interval`` is honoured, clamped to 1..60 seconds, and the
  first poll waits one interval (RFC 8628 §3.5).  ``expires_in`` is clamped to
  30 minutes; S03 uses 10.
* Temporary trouble -- a dropped connection, a 5xx, a 429, a reply that is not
  JSON (a captive

m2c/src/m2c/checkpoints.py -- Patch C08: checkpoints and rewind.

Before an edit, ``snapshot()`` saves what the affected files looked like.
``rewind()`` puts the project back to the state just before a given step ran.
A bug here destroys the user's files, so this module is written around its
failure paths; the happy path is the short part.

What is stored, and where
-------------------------
* **Blobs**: ``~/.m2c/checkpoints/<session>/<sha256>`` (through ``paths``, so
  ``$M2C_HOME`` is honoured).  One file per distinct content, named by the
  SHA-256 of its bytes, so identical content is stored once per session
  (deduplication).  Directories are 0700, blobs 0600, whatever the umask.
  Every blob is written to a temp file in the same directory, flushed,
  ``fsync``ed and renamed into place, so a blob is either whole or absent.
* **The index**: one row per file per step in the C02 store's ``checkpoints``
  table, ``(session_id, step, path, blob_hash, ts, mode)``.  ``path`` is
  relative to the project root and uses ``/``.  ``blob_hash`` is NULL when the
  file **did not exist** before the step (so a rewind deletes it); ``mode`` is
  the permission bits, NULL exactly then.  ``mode`` is the one column this
  patch adds (migration v2 in store/migrations.py).  There is no index outside
  the store.

``snapshot(session_id, step, paths, root)``
-------------------------------------------
Call it *before* the step changes the files.  For each path:

* a regular file: its bytes go in

Deliberately thin.  The client has three knobs so far, all environment
variables so nothing about them is written to disk:

    M2C_HOME        relocates the config directory (documented in paths.py)
    M2C_LOG_LEVEL   DEBUG | INFO | WARNING | ERROR | CRITICAL (default WARNING)
    M2C_SERVER_URL  where the MiniMe backend lives (added by Patch C03; C01
                    had no server setting).  There is no default: the public
                    address is not decided yet, so ``m2c login`` asks for it.
                    After a login the address is stored with the credential,
                    so later commands do not need the variable.

Later work packages (the store in C02, login in C03, the device link in
C04) read their settings through ``Config`` rather than reaching into
``os.environ`` themselves, so tests can pass a plain dict.

Failure policy follows the repo-wide rule: a bad *log level* falls back to
the default (logging fails open and must never stop the CLI), while a bad
*M2C_HOME* raises ``paths.ConfigDirError`` (it decides where credentials
are stored, so it fails closed).  A bad *M2C_SERVER_URL* fails closed too
(``ServerUrlError``): it decides where the device credential is sent.

m2c/src/m2c/context/instructions.py -- Patch C12: hierarchical instruction files
(M2C.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) with ``@path`` imports.

What this produces
------------------
``load_instructions(root, cwd, home)`` returns the text for the ``instructions``
field of ``run.start`` (protocol/v1/run.start.json), plus the list of files it
came from and a list of *notes* about anything that was skipped or cut.  Nothing
is sent anywhere by this module; it only reads files (product guide section 9,
build plan C12).

Order, and what "takes precedence" means
----------------------------------------
Content is concatenated from the LEAST specific source to the MOST specific:

    1. the global file          <M2C home>/M2C.md   (M2C_HOME is honoured, see paths.py)
    2. the repository root      M2C.md, then AGENTS.md, then CLAUDE.md
    3. every directory below the root down to the session's working directory,
       each with the same three names in the same order

A later block overrides an earlier one by being later (models weight what they
read last).  Only ``M2C.md`` is read from the global directory.  Directories that
are not on the way from the root to the cwd are never read.

  (so ``someone@example.com`` and URLs such as ``.../@user/x`` are not imports);
* is not inside a fenced code block (``` or ~~~) or an inline code sp

m2c/src/m2c/context/memory.py -- Patch C12: the project's auto-memory index and
memory writes that the user approves first.

Where memory lives
------------------
Memory is plain files on this device, one directory per project:

    <M2C home>/memory/<project-key>/MEMORY.md        the index (sent as ``memory_index``)
    <M2C home>/memory/<project-key>/<topic>.md       topic files (not sent by this module)

``<M2C home>`` is ``~/.m2c`` unless ``M2C_HOME`` says otherwise (paths.py).  The
project key is ``<slug>-<12 hex digits>``: the slug is the repository folder's
name (lower-case ASCII, unsafe characters turned into ``-``, at most 40
characters) and the digits are the start of the SHA-256 of the repository
root's REAL path (symbolic links resolved, so two ways of reaching the same
folder share one memory).  The key is therefore stable between runs, readable
in a directory listing, and different for two projects that happen to share a
folder name.  It is keyed by location: moving or renaming the repository starts
a new, empty memory (the old directory stays and can be moved by hand).  A git
remote was rejected as the key because many repositories have none and it would
put a URL in a directory name.

The index sent to the server
----------------------------
``load_memory_index`` returns the first 200 lines or the first 25 KB (25 * 1024
bytes) of ``MEMORY.md``, whichever is smaller.  Cuts happen on a line boundary
and never inside a UTF-8 character; ``truncated`` and a ``trunc

m2c/src/m2c/context/rules.py -- Patch C12: path-scoped instruction rules.

Where rules live
----------------
    <M2C home>/rules/*.md        global rules      (id ``global/<name>``)
    <repo>/.m2c/rules/*.md       project rules     (id ``project/<name>``)

Only ``*.md`` files directly inside those directories count (no recursion, no
dotfiles).  Global rules come first, then project rules, each group sorted by
file name, so the order is deterministic and more specific rules come later.
Rules are INSTRUCTION text for the model.  They are not permission rules; those
live in the policy engine (C06) and never leave the device.

File format
-----------
A rule may start with a front-matter block listing the paths it applies to:

    ---
    paths:
      - "src/**/*.py"
      - tests/**
    ---
    Prefer dataclasses over dicts for structured data.

A rule without ``paths`` (or without a front-matter block) applies everywhere.
Accepted forms of ``paths``: a block list (indented or not), a flow list
``[a, "b", 'c']`` (commas inside quotes or ``{braces}`` do not split), or one
scalar pattern.  Other keys (``description:`` ...) are accepted and ignored.
There is no YAML dependency: this is a small parser for exactly these shapes.

Malformed front matter is never a crash: that one rule is skipped and a
``bad_front_matter`` note says why (the note never repeats file content).  These
all count as malformed: a block that is never closed, ``paths`` with no
pattern, an empty or over-long (2

m2c/src/m2c/interact/question.py -- Patch L01a: ``ask_user``, the request, the answer and their rules.

The model asks one question and waits.  It may offer up to six options (each a short label and an optional line of
explanation) and may allow the person to answer in their own words.  The call ends in one of four ways, and the
runner turns each into a ``tool_result``:

    answered   ``ok`` true; the text built here by ``answer_text`` ("The person answered." and then one
               ``Chose: <label>`` line per option and a ``Wrote: <words>`` line);
    declined   ``ok`` false, fixed text (the person closed the question without answering);
    timed out  ``ok`` false, fixed text (``timeout_s`` passed with no answer);
    no person  ``ok`` false, fixed text (headless run, or a screen that cannot ask).

The functions here are pure.  ``parse_question`` is the second line of defence behind the policy engine's type check
(C06 only knows an argument's JSON type, not "at most six options" or "labels are unique") and the first line of
defence for the rules a JSON schema cannot say.  It raises ``QuestionError`` with a FIXED message that names the rule
and never repeats what the model wrote.  ``answer_text`` is the check on the OTHER side: the screen is code too, and
a buggy or hostile one must not be able to put an option the model never offered, or a type that is not text, into
the model's context.

m2c/src/m2c/interact/tasks.py -- Patch L01a: the ``tasks`` list, its validation and the interface a screen implements.

The model keeps a task list for the work in hand and sends the WHOLE list on every call; the new list replaces the old
one and an empty list clears it.  ``parse_tasks`` turns the arguments into a tuple of frozen ``Task`` values or fails
closed with a FIXED message that names the rule and never repeats an id or a title (they are the model's text).

What a JSON schema cannot say is checked here: ids are unique, every ``depends_on`` names a task in the same list and
the dependencies do not form a cycle.  The rules run in a fixed order and the first one that fails is reported:

    list shape -> too many -> each task (shape, id, title, status, depends_on) -> duplicate ids ->
    unknown dependency -> cycle

The list is shown to the person by a ``TaskSink`` (the screen; L01b implements one for the terminal UI) and recorded in
the local event store (type ``tasks``, see the runner).  A task's title is text the model wrote and goes to a terminal,
so it holds no control characters and is a single line.

Standard library only.

Place this file at: m2c/src/m2c/interact/tasks.py

m2c/src/m2c/link/client.py -- Patch C04: the device link, the WebSocket
client that keeps this machine connected to the MiniMe server.

WHAT IT IS
----------
``DeviceLink`` is the one long-lived connection of build plan section 7 / P00
(protocol/README.md).  It does the plumbing so that the rest of the client can
think in runs and events:

* connects to ``wss://<server>/v1/code/device`` and says ``hello`` with the
  device credential (C03's ``load_credential()``); there is no JWT on the
  socket, the credential itself authenticates it.  It then insists on a valid
  ``welcome`` and refuses a server whose ``min_protocol`` is above anything
  this client speaks (``LinkProtocolUnsupportedError``);
* reconnects by itself with exponential backoff and full jitter
  (reconnect.py), stopping for good on ``unauthorized``, ``device_revoked``,
  ``protocol_unsupported`` and being superseded by a newer connection;
* after every (re)connect sends ``run.resume{last_seq}`` for each active run
  and keeps the local event log exactly equal to the server's stream: no
  duplicate, no missing, no out-of-order event (see below);
* correlates requests and answers (ping/pong by nonce, ``error`` by

m2c/src/m2c/link/reconnect.py -- Patch C04: when to try again, how long to
wait, and which failures mean "stop for good".

The device link (client.py) holds one WebSocket to the server for as long as the
person is working.  Networks drop, laptops sleep, servers restart, so the link
reconnects by itself -- but a loop that keeps retrying a revoked device is a
bug, so this module also decides what ends the loop.

THE BACKOFF: exponential, FULL jitter, capped
---------------------------------------------
After the n-th failure in a row the next wait is drawn uniformly from
``[0, min(cap, base * factor**n))`` -- "full jitter".  The usual alternative,
"the delay plus a little noise", leaves many clients that were dropped by the
same server restart retrying in near lock-step; spreading each wait over the
whole interval spreads the herd.  Defaults: base 1 s, factor 2, cap 30 s.

The sequence is reset only by a connection that *actually stayed up*
(``stable_after_s``, 10 s by default).  A server that accepts the handshake and
drops the socket at once must not hold the delay at its minimum: that would be
a tight retry loop with extra steps.  A connect that never got as far as
``welcome`` has not stayed up either.

The random source and the clock are parameters (``Backoff(rng=...)``, and the
link's ``clock=``/``sleep=``), so tests are instant and exact.

A server that says how long to wait (``error rate_limited``,
``details.retry_after_s``) sets a FLOOR for the next delay: the wait is t

message content.

The rule (build plan §11.4, applied to the client): nothing the user typed,
nothing the model produced and nothing a tool returned may appear in a log
line -- not in the message, not in a %-style argument, not in an ``extra=``
field, not inside a traceback.  Logs are what people paste into bug reports,
so "we only meant to log the id" is not good enough; the logging setup
itself has to make the leak impossible rather than rely on every future

   things §11.4 says the server may log.  Values must be numbers, booleans
   or short identifier-like strings; anything else becomes ``<redacted>``.

   never add one that can carry user text.

   records produced by plain ``logger.info(...)`` calls:
   * %-style / mapping arguments are discarded -- the literal template is
     logged, the values never are (``log.info("user said %s", text)``

m2c/src/m2c/paths.py -- Patch C01: where M2C keeps its files on this device.

Per build plan §O1 the device is the source of truth, so everything the
client stores (the SQLite state database from C02, the device credential
from C03, logs, checkpoints, memory ...) goes under one directory:

    ~/.m2c/                     the default
    $M2C_HOME                   overrides it, when set and non-empty

``M2C_HOME`` exists so that tests (and anyone running two profiles side by
side) never touch the real home directory.  Rules for the variable:

* It must be an absolute path (``~`` is expanded first).  A relative path is
  rejected rather than silently resolved against whatever the current
  directory happens to be, because that would scatter credentials around.
* Set but empty counts as unset, the usual shell convention.
* It names the directory itself, not its parent: ``M2C_HOME=/tmp/x`` means
  files land in ``/tmp/x/state.db``, not ``/tmp/x/.m2c/state.db``.
* Parent directories that do not exist are created with default
  permissions; only the final directory is forced to mode 0700.

The directory will hold a device credential, so this module is a *security*
check and fails closed (build plan §0.2).  ``ensure_config_dir`` raises
``ConfigDirError`` instead of carrying on when the directory

* exists but is not a directory,
* is owned by a different user (for example ``sudo m2c`` with a user's HOME),
* or cannot be put into mode 0700 -- typically because the filesystem
  ignor

    decide(request, context) -> Decision(action, reason, matched_rule, ...)

``action`` is ``allow``, ``ask`` or ``deny``.  The function is PURE (no file or
network access, no clock, no logging, no printing) and TOTAL (it never raises:

  anything above R1).  Every ``allow`` is created by one of two functions

  the basis and downgrades anything unexplained to ``deny``.

engine knows, and the default decision per (mode, tool class, risk).

Modes (product guide 8.2, protocol ``common.json#/$defs/mode``):

    plan           reads allowed; every mutation DENIED (``plan_exit`` is the
                   way out, and it asks); no shell.
    ask            reads allowed; edits, deletes and shell ask.   (the default)
    accept-edits   edits to non-protected paths INSIDE the project are allowed;
                   deletes and shell still ask.

A mode default answers only "what happens when no rule says anything".  It can
return ``allow`` in exactly three cases, all for tools that cannot run a process
or reach the network: a read tool at risk R0 (every mode), an edit tool at
risk R1 inside the project in ``accept-edits``, and (Patch L01a) an interact tool
at risk R0 (every mode).  A mode default NEVER allows
network access or process execution: the shell class has no allow entry at all,
and anything above the class ceiling (R3 network or outside the project, R4
irreversible) falls back to ``ask``.  ``tests/policy/test_policy_invariants.py``
enumerates the table to prove that.

The catalog below is a hard-coded copy of ``protocol/v1/tools/*.json`` (P00):
tool name, risk (and ``risk_max`` for ``delete_path``) and the closed set of
arguments.  It is a copy so that deciding never reads a file, and a test fails
if it drifts from the JSON.  The client's risk may RAISE a call's

m2c/src/m2c/policy/rules.py -- Patch C06: permission rules, their layers, and the
purely lexical path checks the policy engine shares.

A rule is ``tool(pattern)`` and has an action, ``deny``, ``ask`` or ``allow``::

    bash(git status)        exact command
    bash(git diff:*)        "git diff" and anything after it (word boundary)
    read_file(src/**)       a path pattern
    edit_file(*.md)         a pattern without a slash also matches the file name

Matching (build plan C06, product guide 8.3):

* Exact strings first, then simple patterns.  ``*`` is the ONLY wildcard and
  matches any run of characters, ``/`` included, so ``src/**`` and ``src/*``
  mean the same.  There is no regular expression anywhere in this module.
* Evaluation order is deny, then ask, then allow, across the UNION of all
  layers (managed, then user, then project).  Because the order is applied to
  the union, a lower layer can never weaken a higher layer: a project ``allow``
  cannot beat a managed ``deny`` or ``ask``, whatever the layer order says.
* Project settings count only when the project is trusted
  (``merge_layers(..., project_trusted=True)``); when it is not, the project
  layer is dropped without being looked at.  The trust prompt itself is built
  later; this module only takes the flag.

Loading is the one place this module touches the disk, and only for the files
the caller names (``load_rule_file`` / ``load_layers`` take paths as arguments,
so tests never read the real home director

m2c/src/m2c/policy/shellparse.py -- Patch C06: a real tokenizer for the subset of
shell syntax the policy engine has to understand.

This is NOT a regex scorer (MiniLocker's engine, which this patch deliberately
does not port, scored command text with regexes and treated syntax it could not
parse as low risk).  It is a small hand-written scanner whose one rule is:

    Anything it cannot classify with certainty is "unknown syntax", and the
    engine turns unknown syntax into ``ask``.  It never turns it into ``allow``.

``parse(command)`` never raises.  It returns a ``ParseResult``: the simple
commands ("parts") found anywhere in the text, in execution order, plus the
reasons (fixed strings, never the command) why some of it is unknown.

What it understands
-------------------
* Separators ``&&  ||  ;  |  |&  &`` and newlines; a part is one simple command.
* Single quotes, double quotes and backslash escapes, and dequoting of words, so
  ``c'u'rl``, ``\curl`` and ``"cur"l`` are all the word ``curl``.  Separators
  inside quotes do not split.
* Subshells ``( )`` and groups ``{ ... ; }`` (flattened: their commands are parts).
* Redirections ``> >> < >| <> &> &>> >& <&`` with an optional fd (``2>&1``) and
  the target word of each.
* Command substitution ``$(...)`` and backticks, nested to a fixed depth: the
  inner text is parsed and its commands become parts that run BEFORE the
  command that contains them.  Substitutions inside double quotes and inside
  ``${...}`` are found

m2c/repl.py -- the walking skeleton's prompt loop (patch I01, "hello run").

WHAT THIS IS. The smallest terminal front end that joins C02 (local store), C03 (login) and
C04 (device link) to the server's text-only turn runner: after login, ``m2c`` shows a prompt;
each line you type is one message; the reply is printed as it streams. The real terminal UI is
C09 and replaces this module; nothing here adds a dependency (plain ``input()``, ``print``,
asyncio and threading from the standard library).

THE FLOW
  * The first message of a conversation starts a run: ``DeviceLink.start_run`` (profile
    "code", mode "ask", ``cwd_label`` = the folder's NAME, never a path). C04 creates the
    session in the local store in the same call. Every later message is
    ``DeviceLink.send_user_message``. Before it goes out, the message is appended to the local
    log as the client event ``user.message`` (the device log is the record; C04 skips non-server
    events when it recovers its resume cursor).
  * ``LinkCallbacks.on_event`` prints each ``text_delta`` as it arrives. C04 has already
    appended every server event to the local store before the callback runs.

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/bridge.py -- Patch C11b: the bridge that gives a sandboxed command a proxy to talk to.

WHAT THIS FILE IS
-----------------
C11a runs a shell command in a bubblewrap sandbox whose network namespace is UNSHARED: the command has loopback and
nothing else.  C11b gives it *controlled* network without ever giving it a network:

    command --HTTP CONNECT--> 127.0.0.1:3128 (this bridge, inside the sandbox)
            --unix socket---> proxy on the host (netproxy.py), which decides, resolves, pins and connects.

The bridge is deliberately dumb.  It relays bytes between a TCP connection on the sandbox's own loopback and the unix
socket that the host proxy listens on.  It decides nothing, reads nothing and logs nothing; every decision is made by
the proxy on the host, so a command that talks to the unix socket directly, or kills the bridge and starts its own,
gains nothing.  A program that ignores the proxy settings simply cannot connect: there is no route (fail closed by
construction).

TWO ROLES IN ONE FILE
---------------------
* As a MODULE (imported by m2c): the constants, ``NetworkMount``, ``proxy_environment`` / ``apply_proxy_environment``
  (the variables injected into the command's environment AFTER sanitizing) and ``launcher_argv``.
* As a SCRIPT (copied by the proxy into its private directory, mounted read-only into the sandbox and run by the
  system ``python3`` there):  ``python3 -I bridge.py --port P --sock PATH -- COMMAND...``.  It binds
  127.0.0.1

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/bwrap.py -- Patch C11a: finding bubblewrap and building the full command.

SECURITY-CRITICAL.  ``profile.build_profile`` says WHAT the sandbox is; this module says how to
start it.  ``tools/shell.py`` calls ``wrap_command`` and runs what it returns exactly as it ran
``[shell, "-c", command]`` before: the same ``subprocess.Popen`` with ``start_new_session=True``,
so C07's process-group kill, timeout, cancel, streaming and output cap are untouched.  Why that
still works: the process the shell tool signals is bubblewrap itself, the leader of the new
session; bubblewrap is also PID 1's parent, and when it dies (SIGKILL included) the kernel kills
every process in the sandbox's PID namespace.  A command that calls ``setsid`` or traps SIGTERM
therefore cannot outlive the call, which is the gap C07 documented and this patch closes.

The command line is ``[bwrap, *profile, "--", shell, "-c", command]``: a list, the command is ONE
element, nothing is quoted or joined, and the double dash makes sure a command that starts with
``-`` is never read as a bubblewrap option.

``find_bwrap`` looks only in ABSOLUTE ``PATH`` entries.  A relative entry (``.``, an empty
element, ``bin``) would let a file in the project directory be found first; a project is the
model's workspace, so it must never be a place a binary is picked up from.

convention) instead of dying by that signal, so the s

THE RULES (pure, no I/O except the one saved file)
--------------------------------------------------
The allowlist holds EXACT hosts (``pypi.org``), explicit wildcards (``*.example.com``) and exact IP literals.

* A wildcard matches any host UNDER the name, at any depth, and never the bare name: ``*.example.com`` matches
  ``a.example.com`` and ``a.b.example.com`` but not ``example.com``.  A wildcard needs at least two labels after the
  star (``*.com`` is ignored), and nothing else with a star is valid.  The star cannot know public suffixes, so a
  person who writes ``*.co.uk`` has allowed a lot; that is theirs to decide.
* Names are lowercased, IDNA-normalized (what is shown and compared is the ASCII/punycode form, so a look-alike
  domain in another script can never be mistaken for the real one on screen) and have no trailing dot.
* IP literals are DENIED unless the exact address is listed (never asked about).  Odd spellings of an address
  (``2130706433``, ``0x7f.1``, ``127.1``) are denied outright.  ``localhost`` and ``*.localhost`` are denied too.
* Only the allowed destination ports pass (443 by default); any other port is denied before anything else.

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/netproxy.py -- Patch C11b: the host-side proxy that decides where a sandboxed command may connect.

THE DESIGN
----------
The sandbox keeps NO direct network (``--unshare-net`` stays).  On the host an asyncio proxy listens on a UNIX socket
inside a private temporary directory (mode 0700, owned by the user).  That directory is bind-mounted READ-ONLY into
the sandbox together with ``bridge.py``; inside, the bridge relays 127.0.0.1:3128 to the socket.  A program that
ignores the proxy settings cannot connect at all: fail closed by construction.  Everything that matters is decided
HERE, on the host, where the command cannot reach the code or its memory.

WHAT THE PROXY DOES, per connection
-----------------------------------
1. Reads the request head (request line and headers up to the blank line) under a total deadline and size caps
   (slowloris and oversized-header protection).  It looks at the request line only; headers are skipped, never
   parsed, stored or logged, and the payload that follows is never looked at.
2. Accepts ``CONNECT host:port`` only.  Plain ``http://`` requests get a fixed 403 (cleartext is OFF by default;
   ``ProxyConfig.allow_cleartext`` turns it on, and then the proxy reads the host out of the request line, nothing
   else, and tunnels the rest blindly).  Every other method gets a fixed 405.
3. Asks the policy (netpolicy.py): allowlist, ports (443 only by default), IP literals, the person's prompt.

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/profile.py -- Patch C11a: the bubblewrap profile.

SECURITY-CRITICAL.  ``build_profile`` turns "run a command for this project" into the
list of ``bwrap`` options that confine it.  It is a pure function: it looks at the
disk (to see what exists) and starts nothing, so every property below is testable on
a machine without bubblewrap.  What it returns is ARGV, a list of strings, never a
shell string: nothing here is ever joined, quoted or parsed by a shell.

What the sandbox is
-------------------
A new root filesystem (a tmpfs bubblewrap makes), into which these are mounted, in
this order (a LATER mount wins over an earlier one at the same place, which is why
the order is part of the contract and tests pin it):

1.  ``/usr`` read-only; ``/bin``, ``/sbin``, ``/lib``, ``/lib64`` as symlinks into
    it when the machine has the merged-``/usr`` layout, as read-only binds of the
    real directory when it does not (``SystemLayout``).
2.  A short, explicit list of ``/etc`` entries (``ETC_ENTRIES``), read-only, each
    only if it exists: passwd, group, ld.so.cache, alternatives, certificates and a
    few more.  NOT ``/etc`` as a whole: ``shadow``, ``ssh``, ``ssl/private`` and
    the system start-up files are simply not there.
3.  A minimal ``/proc`` (of the new PID namespace, so the host's processes are not
    in it), a minimal ``/dev``, and a private, empty, writable ``/tmp``.
4.  The home directory, as an EMPTY tmpfs, made read-only at the end.  The home

Everything the model reads about this machine travels in ``tool_result.output`` and ``tool_stream.chunk``, and the

m2c/src/m2c/store/events.py -- Patch C02: the append-only event log.

``events(session_id, seq, ts, type, json)`` is the device log, the source of
truth for what happened in a session (build plan §O1).  The server's
in-flight buffer may expire; this record does not.  This module is the way
to add to it, read it back and export it.

Appending
---------
``append_event`` and ``append_events`` assign the next ``seq`` for the
session *inside one transaction*: ``db.transaction`` takes the write lock
first (``BEGIN IMMEDIATE``), then the helper reads ``MAX(seq)`` and inserts
``MAX + 1``.  Two writers, in two threads or two processes, therefore cannot
read the same maximum; one waits for the other (up to the busy timeout) and
the seqs come out unique and contiguous, 1, 2, 3 ...  If the caller is
already inside ``db.transaction`` the append joins it as a savepoint, so an
event and, say, an ``approvals`` row commit together; if that outer
transaction rolls back, the seq is not consumed (no gaps).

``seq`` here is the *local* order of this session's log.  It starts at 1 like
the protocol's server stream (protocol/v1/README.md §4) but is not required
to equal it; C04 decides whether to record the server's ``seq`` inside the
payload.

The payload may be any JSON value.  It is serialised first, before the
transaction starts, so an unserialisable payload (``TypeError``) or a NaN
(``ValueError``) never leaves a half-written batch or holds the lock.  It is
stored as *canonical* JSON text: sor

m2c/src/m2c/store/migrations.py -- Patch C02: the schema and its forward-only
migrations.

Versioning
----------
The schema version lives in a table, ``schema_version``, with one row per
migration ever applied::

    schema_version(version INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, applied_at TEXT)

The current version is the highest row; **version 0** is a database that has
no such table (a new, empty file).  A table rather than ``PRAGMA
user_version`` so that the history (which migration, when) is data a later
``m2c doctor`` (C21: "stale or incompatible state migrations") can list.
The table is created by ``migrate()`` itself, in the same transaction as the
first migration, so a migration body never has to know about it.

Rules
-----
* **Forward only.**  There are no down-migrations.  ``migrate(target=n)``
  with ``n`` below the current version raises ``StoreError``.
* **One transaction per migration**, taken with ``BEGIN IMMEDIATE``: the
  schema change and its ``schema_version`` row commit together or not at
  all.  SQLite DDL is transactional, so a migration that fails half way
  leaves the database exactly as it was, at the previous version.  Earlier
  migrations in the same call stay applied.
* **Re-checked under the lock.**  If two processes open a new database at
  once, the loser waits for the write lock, sees the winner's row and skips
  that migration.  Each migration is applied exactly once.
* **An up-to-date database is not written to.**  ``migrate()`` reads the
  version

denylist for the local tool executors.

Ported from daemon/path_guard.py (MiniMe, 6977ddf) and extended.  The daemon
module is untouched and nothing here imports it; ``assert_safe_root``,
``is_within_root`` and ``assert_within_root`` keep the daemon's names, signatures
and messages (the 14 daemon tests run unchanged against them, see
tests/tools/test_tools_path_guard_port.py).  What C05 adds is everything the
daemon's guard did not need while it only listed and read files:

* a **resolver per intent** (``resolve_for_read`` / ``_write`` / ``_delete``)
  that returns a project-relative path made of *real* components, so the rest
  of the executor never handles a string it has to re-check;
* the **denylist**, in two forms (below);
* **no-follow opening** (``open_dir_chain``, ``open_regular``) that closes the
  gap between "the path was checked" and "the path was opened".

Containment (what ``resolve_*`` enforces)
-----------------------------------------
* Everything is pinned under the session root.  Relative paths are joined to
  it; absolute paths are accepted only if they land inside it, exactly like a
  relative one would.  ``~`` is *not* expanded in a tool argument (a file may be

m2c/src/m2c/tools/search.py -- Patch C05: glob and grep.

Ported from daemon/tools.py (MiniMe, 6977ddf) in spirit only: the daemon had no
search tools, so these are new.  Nothing is imported from ``daemon/``.

glob
----
Pure Python, no subprocess.  The pattern is matched segment by segment against
the paths under the search directory (``*``, ``?``, ``[...]`` per segment, and a
whole segment ``**`` for "any number of directories, including none").  A
pattern without a ``/`` therefore matches the top level only; the "no files
matched" message says so, because that is the mistake models make.  The walk

* never follows a symlinked directory and never enters ``.git``;
* omits every protected entry (hard and user lists) and does not descend into a
  protected directory;
* lists a symlink only if its real target is a regular file inside the project
  that is not protected;
* is capped by entries scanned (``caps.glob_max_walk_entries``) and by time
  (``caps.glob_timeout_s``), and the result is capped by ``max_results``;
* returns a sorted list (plain code-point order of the project-relative path),
  so the same tree gives the same answer every time.

Ignore files are not read (see the patch notes).

grep
----
A wrapper around ripgrep (``rg``), which is an external tool: nothing is
installed and nothing is imported.  The model controls three things: a regular
expression, a path, and a file-name glob.  None of them may become a ripgrep
*option*, so:

* The argument vector is built in

SECURITY-CRITICAL
-----------------
Patch C11a (the sandbox, ``m2c.sandbox``) changes WHERE the command runs, not how a call
is checked or supervised: when a working sandbox is available the command runs inside
bubblewrap (project writable, ``.git``, ``.m2c`` and shell rc files read-only, an empty
home, no network, its own PID namespace); when it is not, it runs as described below, with
the user's full privileges, and the visible warning says so.  See "The sandbox" at the end
of this docstring.  The rest of this text is C07's and still holds in both cases.

This module runs a command the model proposed, as the user.  Without the sandbox it can
read and write anything the user can, use the network and start other programs; the only
things between the model and the user's account are then the approval flow (C06 decides,
the device runner and the terminal UI ask) and the checks in this file, which exist to make sure that

* nothing runs unless the caller says, explicitly, that it was authorized;
* a policy ``deny`` still wins over that authorization;
* the command cannot outlive its time limit or its cancel handle;
* the command does not inherit the user's credentials from the environment;
* its output cannot flood memory or inject escape codes into the terminal UI.

first command of a session that runs WITHOUT a sandbox (``warn

Why
---
A project folder is attacker-controlled content (a cloned repository), and a few of its files are *configuration with power*:
settings that can allow commands without asking, hooks that run commands, skills that add instructions the model follows.

m2c/src/m2c/trust/prompt.py -- Patch C26: the folder-trust prompt as a pure key state machine, what it shows, and the status
note for a folder that is not trusted.

Like tui/approval.py, this is the pure part: what the prompt shows (``describe_prompt``), what each key means
(``TrustPromptMachine``), and the one-line note (``ignored_note``).  The terminal layer (tui/session.py) only forwards keys
and shows blocks.

KEYS
----
``t`` trust this folder and remember it (until its files change) · ``s`` trust it for this session only, remember nothing ·
``n`` do not trust it, and remember that (until its files change) · Esc the same as ``n``.  Any other key does nothing: no
key ever answers by accident (Enter, Space and Tab included), and the machine answers at most once.  Closing m2c with the
question open answers nothing and remembers nothing, so the person is asked again next time.

-------------
The folder, how many files and which (the names come from the project, so every one is cleaned of terminal control
characters and cut), a plain-language warning, and the keys.  The list is cut at MAX_FILES_SHOWN names with a count of the rest.

m2c/src/m2c/trust/store.py -- Patch C26: the folder-trust store (``<M2C home>/trust.json``) and the trust decision.

What is stored
--------------
One small JSON file mapping the CANONICAL absolute project root (its real path, so a symlinked path and the real path are the
same folder) to what the person decided and for which files:

    {"version": 1,
     "folders": {"/home/me/code/app": {"decision": "trusted" | "untrusted",
                                       "fingerprint": "<64 hex, see fingerprint.py>",
                                       "time": <seconds since the epoch>}}}

A decision is only ever valid for the fingerprint it was made for.  Any change to a trust-relevant file (a ``git pull`` that
edits a hook, say) changes the fingerprint, so the old answer no longer applies and the person is asked again.  An explicit
"untrusted" is remembered the same way, so the person is not asked again for the same files.

How the file is protected (it is a security file: a forged "trusted" entry would switch on a folder's hooks)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
* It lives in the M2C home (mode 0700, tightened by ``paths.ensure_config_dir``), created 0600, written atomically: a temp file
  in the same directory (mode 0600 from the start), flushed and fsynced, then renamed over the old file.  A crash leaves the old
  file or the new one, never half of one.
* Reading REFUSES a file that is not a regular file

m2c/src/m2c/tui/complete.py -- Patch C09a: ``@`` file mentions.

Typing ``@`` in the message line completes project file paths.  It only INSERTS the relative path into the message;
it never reads or attaches contents.  What is offered is decided here (pure logic plus a bounded directory scan);
the prompt_toolkit ``Completer`` that calls it lives in app.py.

WHAT IS NEVER OFFERED
---------------------
* Anything C05's denylist blocks (``Denylist.blocks`` on the root-relative parts: ``.env``, keys, M2C's own state
  directory, the user's patterns), and the directory is not entered either.
* ``.git`` (and ``node_modules``, ``__pycache__``: they would use up the scan budget).
* Symbolic links of any kind (a link can point outside the project or at a protected file; the scan neither offers
  nor follows them).  Each candidate is also run through C05's ``resolve_for_read`` as a last check.
* Names with control or format characters (they would put hidden text into the message line).

BOUNDS
------
The scan stops after ``MAX_FILES`` files or ``TIME_BUDGET_S`` seconds, whichever comes first (the loop it runs on
also carries the device link), and a query returns at most ``MAX_CANDIDATES`` paths.  ``Scan.complete`` says whether
the whole tree was seen.

m2c/src/m2c/tui/grant.py -- Patch C09a: asking for more credits when a run is paused for budget (``g``).

``POST /v1/code/runs/{run_id}/grant`` (S10) raises the run's credit ceiling when the run is in ``paused_budget`` and
the account's pool has room.  The device authenticates with its short-lived access token (C03's
``get_access_token()``); the answer is numbers and a state word.  This module makes that one call with the standard
library and turns every outcome into a ``GrantResult`` and one fixed sentence (``describe``).

SAFETY
------
* The token is revealed only to build the ``Authorization`` header; it is never logged, printed or put in a result.
* The server address is the credential's own, run through ``normalize_server_url`` (https, or http to loopback
  only); redirects are NOT followed (a redirect would carry the token elsewhere).
* Nothing the server sends is shown except numbers it must have sent as numbers, a state word of lowercase letters
  and a ``reset_at`` timestamp that matches a strict pattern.  Error ``message`` text is never shown.
* Credits only; no dollars.
* Blocking work (the token fetch and the HTTP call) runs in a thread so the loop that carries the device link keeps
  running.

m2c/src/m2c/tui/history.py -- Patch C09a: the conversation rebuilt from the local log, for ``run.start``'s ``history``.

WHY THIS EXISTS
---------------
P00 has no softer interrupt than ``cancel``, and cancel ends the run.  The conversation is not lost, because the
device keeps it (C02): the next message starts a NEW run and passes ``history`` -- the protocol's history items --
rebuilt from the session's log.  The same happens after a rewind (C08), where the server's copy of the conversation
is out of step with the files.  This module is that rebuild.  It is pure: it reads a sequence of ``(type, data)``
pairs and returns history items; it touches no store and no terminal.

THE LOG CONVENTION (written by the app; ``repl.py`` already writes the first two)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
``user.message {text}`` · ``user.unsent {}`` (the last user message never reached the server) ·
``assistant.message {text}`` (one per model step, written at ``text_done``; a reply that was restarted is written
once, with its final text) · ``tool.call {call_id, tool, input}`` · ``tool.result {call_id, ok, output, truncated?,
trust?}`` (what the device sent back; the run's events carry no outputs) · ``tool.closed {call_id, status}`` (the
server's ``tool_finished``) · ``checkpoint {step, call_id?, tool?}`` (a C08 snapshot step, tied to its call) ·
``rewind {to_step}`` (written by ``checkpoints.rewind``).  Anything else in the log is ignored.

This is the "what is shown" half of the terminal chat; app.py (a later patch) is the thin prompt_toolkit/rich layer
that prints the blocks.  Nothing here touches a terminal, a file or a clock, so every event type can be tested with
plain strings.

BLOCKS
------
``Block.kind`` is ``text`` (append to the current line: a streamed piece of the reply, no newline of its own),
``line`` (one whole line with a ``style``) or ``diff`` (the lines of a diff, collapsed or not).  Styles are names
(``plain dim info warning error user queued assistant tool ok bad``); the UI maps them to colors.

EVERY STRING IS CLEANED HERE
----------------------------

prints blocks cannot show an escape sequence by forgetting to.  Tool and code names are restricted to a safe
alphabet.  Server error messages are never shown (fixed text per code, plus the code), because a message is free
text.

---------------------------------
``text_delta`` pieces are returned as they arrive.  ``reply_restarted`` (a notice from the server: the reply is
being written again after a dropped connection) closes the current line, forgets the partial reply and returns one
short line.  Terminal scrollback cannot be un-printed, so the discarded text stays above that line; what is
discarded is the renderer'

m2c/src/m2c/tui/safe.py -- Patch C09a: making untrusted text safe to show in a terminal.

EVERYTHING THE SERVER OR THE MODEL SENDS IS UNTRUSTED TEXT
----------------------------------------------------------
A model can be steered by a file it read, and a server is only as trustworthy as its last deploy.  Text that reaches
a terminal can recolor it, move the cursor, rewrite earlier lines, set the window title, make a hyperlink or hide
what a command really says (bidirectional overrides).  Every string that came from the server, the model or a file
therefore goes through ``clean`` before it is displayed, and is never handed to a markup interpreter
(``escape_markup`` exists for any caller that must).  The renderer (render.py) does this once, at the door, so no
display code can forget it.

What ``clean`` removes: ANSI/VT escape sequences (CSI, OSC, DCS/SOS/PM/APC, two-character escapes, and the 8-bit C1
forms), every control character except newline and tab (a lone carriage return becomes a newline: it would
overwrite the line), DEL, C1 controls, bidirectional controls and every other "format" character (zero-width
characters, joiners), and lone surrogates.  It never raises and never returns a character that a terminal could
act on.  An escape sequence split across two streamed pieces leaves at most harmless printable letters behind.

Standard library only; pure; no I/O.

m2c/src/m2c/tui/status.py -- Patch C09a: the status line, and the live mode cycle.

``StatusState`` is what the status line knows; ``observe`` folds one server event into it; ``format_status`` and
``status_lines`` turn it into text.  Pure: no terminal, no clock, no I/O.

WHAT THE LINE SHOWS
-------------------
mode · the model (its quality class when known, else the model id of the last usage event) · the TAINTED flag, only
when it is true (C17 comes later, so it is always false for now) · the context percentage · the credits spent in this
run (and the session total when it differs) · "working" and the number of queued messages.  Credits only: no
dollars anywhere.

THE CONTEXT PERCENTAGE IS AN ESTIMATE
-------------------------------------
It is the ``input_tokens`` of the LAST usage event over a window size (a constant, ``M2C_CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS`` can
override it, an unusable value is ignored).  The text says ``~`` and the second line says "approximate".  The server
compacts the context itself, so this is a hint, not a guarantee.

THE QUALITY CLASS
-----------------
The protocol has no quality-class field.  The class reaches a client only inside the fixed text of the
``model_changed`` notice ("... so a <class> model is answering instead."); ``observe`` reads it with a strict
pattern (lowercase letters, at most 24).  Anything else leaves it unknown.  A protocol field would be better; that
is a note for the protocol owner, not something this patch invents.

m2c/tests/auth/mock_server.py -- Patch C03: a scripted stand-in for the S03
device endpoints, plus the helpers the auth tests share.

The server is a real ``http.server`` on 127.0.0.1 (random port), so the tests
drive the genuine ``urllib`` code path in m2c.auth.login: sockets, headers,
redirects, dropped connections and all.  Time is the only thing faked (see
``FakeTime``): the server answers instantly, and the client's sleeps and
deadline run on a clock the test controls, so a "10 minute" login takes
milliseconds.

Scripting.  ``server.script("pair/poll", reply1, reply2, ...)`` queues the
replies for one path; each request pops the next.  When a script runs dry the
request is recorded in ``server.unscripted`` and answered with a 500, and the
``server`` fixture fails the test -- an unexpected extra call is a bug in
either the test or the client.  ``repeat_last=True`` keeps answering with the
final reply (for "pending forever").

The secret constants below are what the mock server hands out.  Each is
distinctive so a leak is unmistakable, and each satisfies the real S03 shapes
(token_urlsafe(32)-like for the codes, three dot-separated parts for the JWT,
a UUID for the device id).

m2c/tests/link/link_fakes.py -- Patch C04: a fake device server and the
helpers the link tests share.

Why this is a plain module and not a conftest.py: tests/test_doctor.py does
``from conftest import ...``, which resolves by module name, and a second
conftest.py in tests/link would shadow the real one (the same reason
tests/auth/auth_fixtures.py exists).  Each test file imports what it needs
from here; the autouse fixtures below are re-exported with ``import *`` and so
apply only to the link tests.

The fake server
---------------
``FakeServer`` is a real ``websockets`` server on 127.0.0.1 with an ephemeral
port, so the client under test runs its genuine network code: handshake,
frames, abrupt connection loss, close codes.  Each connection is handled by a
*script* -- an ``async def script(conn)`` -- chosen by connection number, so a
test says exactly what the server does on the first connection, the second,
and so on.  Ready-made scripts:

    fixture_script(lines)   replays one connection of a P00 golden transcript:
                            for every client line it waits for the client's
                            message and compares it (type, run_id, payload;
                            ids and timestamps are not compared); for every
                            server line it sends it verbatim.
    ReplayRun(events)       a tiny model of the server's resume rule
                            (protocol/README.md section 5): it holds a run's
                            w

"Done when" test of this work package:

    killing the connection mid-stream resumes without duplicate or missing events.

The server side is ``ReplayRun`` (link_fakes.py), which follows the rule of
protocol/README.md section 5: on run.resume{last_seq} re-deliver every event
with seq > last_seq verbatim.  What is checked is the DEVICE LOG, the source of
truth (build plan O1): after however many kills, the stored server events are
exactly seq 1..N once each, in order, and the local sequence has no holes.

Also here: duplicates are ignored by seq, a gap is never stored out of order
(the client asks again from last_seq), last_seq is recovered from the store
after a restart -- including a real SIGKILL of the client process -- and the
details of which runs are resumed and how.

m2c/tests/policy/test_policy_decide_table.py -- Patch C06: the large table.

Three tables, all through ``decide``:

* SHELL: bypass attempts and plain commands against a fixed rule set (BASIC:
  a few explicit allows, a few denies, one ask) or a writers rule set.
* FILES: the file tools in each mode, paths that escape or are protected.
* MODES: the same calls in plan, ask and accept-edits.

A row is ``(command_or_input, expected_action)`` with the rule set named by the
table.  The expected action is the point: an ``allow`` only where the rules say
so, ``deny`` for what a rule or the protected/secret lists forbid, ``ask`` for
everything the engine cannot be sure of.  Some rows were seeded from MiniLocker
54520a2 (tests/test_policy.py); they are marked ``# ML``.

m2c/tests/policy/test_policy_interact.py -- Patch L01a: what C06 decides for ``ask_user`` and ``tasks``.

Neither tool touches a file or runs a command, so both are risk R0 in the catalog and the engine allows them in
every mode with no approval prompt (``ask_user`` IS the prompt).  Everything else the engine does still holds:
a deny rule wins, an ask rule asks, malformed input is denied, nothing is auto-allowed when the settings could
not be read, and a risk above R0 asks.

m2c/tests/policy/test_policy_invariants.py -- Patch C06: "no allow without a rule or a mode".

Done-when item: *no code path allows without an explicit rule or mode.*  Three
independent checks:

1. STATIC.  Read decide.py and list every place the string "allow" can be turned
   into a verdict.  Exactly two functions may create an allow verdict
   (``_allow_rule``, ``_allow_mode``) and ``_finalize`` may only compare it; the
   module-level rank table is the only other mention.  A new allow path added
   later fails this test until the test is edited on purpose.
2. EXHAUSTIVE.  modes.mode_default is enumerated over its whole domain
   (test_policy_modes.py); here the engine's own allow paths are enumerated by
   wrapping the two constructors and running thousands of seeded random calls.
   Every Decision that says allow must have been built by one of them, must name
   its basis, and the basis must hold up when recomputed independently.
3. NEGATIVE.  With no allow rule anywhere, shell, delete and plan_exit are never
   allowed in any mode; in plan mode nothing but a read is ever allowed.

The decision function is also shown to be pure: it opens no file, stats nothing,
resolves no symlink, and writes no log.

m2c/tests/runner/runner_rig.py -- Patch C24: the shared rig of the device tool runner tests.

Why a plain module and not a conftest.py: tests/test_doctor.py does ``from conftest import ...`` (see
tests/headless/headless_rig.py for the same reason).  Each test file imports what it needs from here.

WHAT IS REAL AND WHAT IS FAKE
-----------------------------
Real: the C05 tools (``run_tool`` on a temporary project directory), the C06 policy engine (real rule layers), the
C07 shell tool (real ``bash`` processes), the C08 checkpoints (real blobs under the hermetic ``$M2C_HOME``) and the C02
store (a real SQLite file).  Fake: the link (``FakeLink``: records what the runner sends and checks every payload
against the client's own copy of the protocol schemas, through the link's own strict validator), the person (``ask``
callables the test writes) and, for the ordering tests only, the executor (an injected ``run_tool`` stand-in).

Nothing here looks like a secret: markers are plain words, fake tokens are not needed.

m2c/tests/sandbox/test_netproxy.py -- Patch C11b: the host-side proxy, against a fake resolver and a fake upstream.

Nothing here touches the internet: the resolver is a dict, the "upstream" is an echo server on loopback that the fake
connector reaches no matter what address the proxy pinned (the pinned address is RECORDED, which is the evidence).

What is proven: a denied or unlisted host is never resolved or connected to; private, loopback, link-local/metadata,
CGNAT, unique-local, multicast, reserved and IPv4-mapped destinations are refused even for allowlisted names; DNS is
resolved ONCE and the connection goes to that address (rebinding); one bad address in an answer refuses the whole
answer; plain http and non-CONNECT requests are refused with fixed text; oversized request lines and headers, slow
heads and idle tunnels are cut; connection caps hold; shutdown closes everything and removes the directory; the
test-only loopback flag is reachable from no setting, environment variable or production constructor.

Place this file at: m2c/tests/sandbox/test_netproxy.py

m2c/tests/sandbox/test_sandbox_probe.py -- Patch C11a: the sandbox self-test (``m2c.sandbox.probe``).

Two halves.

1. Logic, with a FAKE runner (no bubblewrap needed, runs everywhere).  ``FakeSandbox`` behaves like a
   correct sandbox: it answers each check's script the way a sandbox that held would (and makes the one
   host-side change the "basic" check expects).  Every failure mode is then one deliberate deviation:
   a leak on the real disk, a leak in the output, a sandbox that does not start (each classified error),
   a hang, a crash, a missing binary, a refused profile.  What is pinned: the probe says "does not work"
   in every one of them and says WHICH check, the result never contains a path or output, the temporary
   world is always removed, and nothing is logged but words and codes.

2. The probe against the REAL bubblewrap, weakened on purpose (marked ``real_sandbox``; skipped loudly
   when bubblewrap or user namespaces are missing).  A probe that passes proves little unless it also
   fails when the sandbox is weak, so each mutation removes one protection from the real command line
   and the matching check, and only that one, must fail.

Run: cd m2c && pytest tests/sandbox/test_sandbox_probe.py -v -rs

m2c/tests/secret_handling/secret_fakes.py -- Patch C15: fake secrets and ordinary developer text, built at run time.

WHY EVERYTHING HERE IS ASSEMBLED WHEN A TEST RUNS
-------------------------------------------------
This repository's pre-commit hook and CI run gitleaks, and m2c/tests/ is not on its allowlist.  So no string in this
directory may look like a real credential as a literal: every fake below is joined from short pieces, or drawn from a
seeded random generator, when it is CALLED.  ``_cat`` is a function on purpose: ``"gh" + "p_" + ...`` in a function
body is folded by the Python compiler into one contiguous constant (and lands in the .pyc file, where gitleaks looks
too), a call to ``_cat`` is not.

The fakes are random, not hand-picked, so the tests exercise the detectors on values nobody chose.  Every random body
is given at least one digit and one letter (``_mixed``): a real 32-character key lacks a digit with a chance below one
in a thousand, and the detectors that need a digit say so in their documentation.

``Fake.secret`` is the part that must never survive redaction; ``Fake.text`` is a realistic line around it.

m2c/tests/secret_handling/test_secrets_corpus.py -- Patch C15: the false-positive budget, stated and enforced.

THE BUDGET
----------
Redaction has two ways to be wrong.  A false negative leaks a credential to the server; it is the failure this whole
patch exists to prevent, so the budget for it is ZERO on every kind the detectors claim: the secret corpus below
(built at run time from random pieces, 30 kinds x 40 seeds) must be caught 100 %.  A false positive hides a harmless
span from the model, which then has to ask the person for it: annoying, never dangerous.  So the budget for it is a
ceiling, not zero, and it is set from how often a developer's tool output is actually hit:

* ``FALSE_POSITIVE_LINE_BUDGET = 0.5 %``: at most one line in two hundred of the ordinary-text corpus may be changed.
  The corpus is deliberately hard (about a third of its lines contain a word like ``password`` or ``token``), so
  real output, which is mostly logs and source with far fewer such words, is hit much less often than that.
* Git commit hashes (any length), SHA-256 digests and UUIDs are NEVER redacted, anywhere in the ordinary text
  (zero tolerance, asserted per category): the model needs them to read ``git log``, lock files and traces.

The categories of ordinary text: git hashes and logs, checksums, UUIDs (also next to credential words), base64 images
(also next to credential words), lock files, minified code, long identifiers, source code full of credential-shaped
words, logs and tra

m2c/tests/secret_handling/test_secrets_runner.py -- Patch C15: redaction at the outbound boundary of the runner.

THE SCRIPTED SESSION
--------------------
Canary secrets (fake, built at run time) are planted in project files and in the environment; a scripted session
runs through C24's real ``ToolRunner`` (real tools, real shell, real policy) against the fake link, which checks every
payload against the protocol schemas.  The assertion that matters: no canary (nor any 8-character window of one)
appears in ANY ``tool_result`` output, ``tool_stream`` chunk or edited-call line the link was handed.

THE OTHER HALF: THE TERMINAL
----------------------------
What the person sees locally is not redacted.  The runner's executor is wrapped by a tap that records what the tools
really produced, and what ``on_chunk`` was given, BEFORE the boundary: those still hold the canaries.  (In this version
the person's terminal shows tool activity from the runner's own callbacks and the server's run events, never from the
outgoing copy; the redaction happens only on the copy that leaves.)

m2c/tests/test_checkpoints.py -- Patch C08: checkpoints and rewind.

A bug in this module can destroy the user's files, so most of what is here is
a failure path: corrupt blobs, symlinks swapped in after the snapshot, paths
that try to leave the project, an index that was edited by hand, a snapshot or
a rewind that is interrupted half way.  The happy path comes first and is
short: edit, edit, rewind, and the bytes are exactly what they were.

Fault injection
---------------
Two small, private functions of ``m2c.checkpoints`` are replaced by tests as
seams, because there is no other way to make a real failure land at exactly
that point:

* ``_insert_rows``  -- the one database transaction that records a step; a
  test makes it fail (or stall, in tests/test_checkpoints_crash.py) *after*
  every blob has been written and *before* any row is.
* ``_apply_item``   -- restores or deletes one file during a rewind; a test
  makes it fail after the first file.

The failure in the *middle* of the transaction needs no seam: it is a
database trigger that aborts the insert of one particular path.

Nothing here looks like a secret: file contents are random bytes or short
marker words, and every hash is computed at run time.

m2c/tests/test_checkpoints_crash.py -- Patch C08: a process that is killed in
the middle of a snapshot or a rewind.

tests/test_checkpoints.py injects failures inside one process.  That proves the
rollback paths; it cannot prove what a SIGKILL leaves on disk, because nothing
runs after one: no ``finally``, no ``atexit``, no rollback, no temp-file
clean-up.  So here a real child process is stopped at the interesting moment
and killed, and this process then looks at what is left.

* ``test_kill_after_the_blobs_before_the_index``: the child has written every
  blob and is about to open the index transaction.  After the kill: the
  database is healthy, the step has no rows at all (not even a partial set),
  the orphan blobs are there and harmless, the same step can be recorded again,
  and ``gc_orphans`` clears the orphans.
* ``test_kill_in_the_middle_of_a_rewind``: the child has restored one file and
  dies.  After the kill, running the same rewind in this process finishes the
  job and ends in exactly the state a clean rewind would have.

The kill points use the same two seams as the in-process tests
(``_insert_rows`` and ``_apply_item``), set inside the child, so no test hook
exists in the production code path.

m2c/tests/test_store_crash.py -- Patch C02: an interrupted write leaves a
valid database.

Each test starts a real child process that talks to the store and kills it
with SIGKILL -- no ``finally``, no ``atexit``, no chance to roll back or
close the connection -- then reopens the database in this process.

* ``test_kill_with_an_open_uncommitted_transaction``: the child begins a
  transaction and writes enough that SQLite spills uncommitted pages to the
  WAL file; after the kill, ``PRAGMA integrity_check`` is ``ok`` and none of
  those rows is visible.
* ``test_kill_in_the_middle_of_a_stream_of_commits``: the child commits
  events one by one and reports each seq on stdout *after* the commit
  returned; after the kill, every reported seq is present and the log has no
  gaps.  (SIGKILL does not lose data the kernel already has, so an
  acknowledged commit must survive; power loss is what ``synchronous=FULL``
  is for and cannot be simulated here.)
